phases.name: Operating rules
phases.aim: The curriculum only works if the process is boring and repeatable. These are habits, not progress — they don't count toward the meter.

items.text: Mon–Thu: learn and build.
Fri: build, debug, write tests.
Sat: independent challenge — no tutorial open.
Sun: rest, or light review only.
Target 4–6 focused hours a day, six days a week.
10 min — write down the outcome for today in one sentence.
45–75 min — study the course, video, or docs.
90–150 min — implement it without copy-pasting.
30–60 min — deliberate problem solving.
30–60 min — push the current project forward.

Reproduce the failure on demand before touching anything.
Read the whole traceback, bottom line first.
Inspect actual state — print, breakpoint, or pdb.
Form one hypothesis and write it down.
Test the hypothesis. Only then search for help.

sections.title: The AI ladder — climb in order

items.text: 1. Explain the concept to me.
2. Give me a hint, not the answer.
3. Diagnose my reasoning, not my code.
4. Review my implementation after it works.
5. Generate adversarial test cases against it.
6. Show an implementation — only after I've attempted it.
Never copy a whole tutorial project and call it finished.
When a concept lands, modify it immediately into something else.
Break your own code on purpose so you learn what failure looks like.
Every serious project gets Git, tests, a README, and a real commit history.
Measure performance. Never guess at it.
80% doing, 20% studying. Early phases 60/40, later phases 90/10.

quizzes.name: Git & environment
quizzes.desc: Version control you can recover from.

questions.prompt: You pushed a commit containing an API key, then made three more commits. What is the correct first move?
choices: Revoke the key, then purge it from history
Purge it with git filter-repo, then force-push
Delete the file in a new commit and push it
Revert the commit that added the key and push
questions.explain: Anyone who fetched, forked or cached the repository already holds the key, and no edit to your history reaches their copies. Only revoking it at the provider makes the leaked value useless; filter-repo and a force-push are the clean-up afterwards.
explain_choice: Rewriting your history does not touch clones, forks or caches that already have the key, so it must be revoked first.
Deleting the file changes only the latest snapshot; every earlier commit still contains the key.
revert adds an inverse commit, so the key stays readable in the original commit for anyone who looks.

questions.prompt: What does `git revert <sha>` do?
choices: Restores the working files to that commit's state
Removes that commit and its changes from the branch's history
Moves the branch pointer back to that commit
Adds a new commit that undoes that commit's changes
questions.explain: History is never rewritten: git computes the inverse of the named commit's diff and records it as a new commit on top. That is why revert is safe on a shared branch and reset is not, since everyone else's clone still agrees with yours.
explain_choice: Restoring files from a commit is git restore --source; it does not create a commit.
That describes rewriting history; revert leaves the original commit in place and adds another.
Moving the branch pointer is what git reset does, which rewrites history.

questions.prompt: You are mid-change on a feature branch and must fix something on main now. What keeps your uncommitted work safe?
choices: Run git restore . for a clean tree, then switch
Stash it, switch, and pop the stash when you return
Just switch; uncommitted edits stay on their branch
Reset --hard; the reflog keeps the discarded edits
questions.explain: Uncommitted changes belong to the working tree, not to any branch, so switching either carries them along or refuses. Stash records them as commits on a separate ref, so they survive the switch and can be reapplied. restore and reset --hard discard them, and the reflog only tracks commits.
explain_choice: restore overwrites the working files, so the unsaved edits are gone for good.
Uncommitted edits are not attached to a branch; they follow you to main or block the switch.
The reflog records commits HEAD pointed at, not uncommitted edits, so reset --hard loses them.

questions.prompt: What is the practical difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
choices: fetch downloads one branch; pull downloads every branch
fetch updates your branch; pull also updates the files
fetch moves only origin/* refs; pull also merges or rebases
fetch only reports new commits; pull downloads them
questions.explain: fetch downloads objects and moves only remote-tracking refs such as origin/main, so nothing you are working on changes. pull runs that fetch and then merges or rebases your current branch onto the result, which is the step that can conflict.
explain_choice: Both fetch every configured branch by default; the difference is the integration step, not the scope.
fetch never moves your local branch; only the integration step in pull does that.
fetch does download the commits; it just stores them under remote-tracking refs instead of your branch.

questions.prompt: Your branch looks 'lost' after a bad `git reset --hard`. What recovers it?
choices: git checkout HEAD~1 to step back before it
Nothing: reset --hard deletes the commits
git reflog, then reset to the SHA it lists
git revert HEAD to undo the reset itself
questions.explain: reset moves the branch pointer but leaves the commits in the object store, and every move of HEAD is logged in the reflog. HEAD@{1} is where you were before the reset; HEAD~1 is the parent commit, which is a different thing. Commits the reflog still points at survive for 30 days by default.
explain_choice: HEAD~1 is the parent in the commit graph, not where HEAD was before; that is HEAD@{1}.
reset only moves a pointer; the commits stay in the object store until garbage collection, weeks later.
revert undoes a commit's changes; a reset is not a commit, so there is nothing for revert to invert.

questions.prompt: Why is a src-layout package preferred over a flat layout?
choices: Relative imports need the package to be inside src/ to work
Tests import the installed package, not the checkout
pip and uv refuse to build a flat-layout project
Python finds modules in src/ faster at import time
questions.explain: In a flat layout the project root is on sys.path when tests run, so `import mypkg` can pick up the source folder even if packaging is broken. Moving the package under src/ takes it off that path, so tests pass only against what was actually installed, missing data files and entry points included.
explain_choice: Relative imports depend on being inside a package, not on where that package sits in the repo.
Build tools handle flat layouts fine; the benefit is what your tests end up importing.
Import speed does not depend on the folder name; the layout changes which copy gets imported.

questions.prompt: What does `uv run script.py` do that `python script.py` doesn't?
choices: Installs whatever the script imports, as it hits them
Compiles the script ahead of time so it starts faster
Activates .venv for the rest of your shell session
Syncs the project's environment, then runs inside it
questions.explain: uv run checks the lockfile and .venv against pyproject.toml, installs whatever is missing or out of date, and runs the command inside that environment for that one process. Dependencies come from the project's declaration, never from scanning imports, and nothing stays activated afterwards.
explain_choice: uv installs what pyproject.toml or inline script metadata declares; it does not watch imports.
The script still runs on the normal interpreter; uv's work is preparing the environment.
The environment applies to that one child process; your shell is left as it was.

questions.prompt: A merge stops with `<<<<<<< HEAD` markers in a file. What do they mean?
choices: Both sides changed these lines; you choose the result
The merge failed, so it must be aborted with --abort and retried
The lines below ======= are your current branch's
Git merged both versions and marks lines to review
questions.explain: A three-way merge compares both tips with their common ancestor; where both changed the same region it cannot choose, so it writes both. Above ======= is HEAD, your current branch; below is the incoming side. Edit to the intended result, delete the markers, then git add the file to mark it resolved.
explain_choice: The merge is paused, not failed; resolving the file and committing completes it.
HEAD, your current branch, is the part above =======; the incoming branch is below it.
Git did not combine these lines; it left both versions for you to reconcile.

quizzes.name: Python foundations
quizzes.desc: The behaviours that trip everyone up early.

questions.prompt: What does `def f(x, items=[])` do wrong?
choices: A new empty list is built on each call, wasting time
One list is made at def time and shared by every call
The default is read-only, so appending raises an error
Nothing, unless two threads call f at the same time
questions.explain: Defaults are evaluated once, when the def statement runs, and stored on the function object in f.__defaults__. Every call that omits items gets that same list, so appends pile up across calls. Default to None and create the list inside the body.
explain_choice: If a fresh list were built per call there would be no bug; the default is evaluated only once.
A list default is an ordinary mutable list, so appending works and silently persists.
One thread is enough: sequential calls already share and mutate the same list.

questions.prompt: `a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a; b.append(4)`. What is `a` now?
choices: [1, 2, 3, 4], because a and b name one list
[1, 2, 3], as its ints are immutable
[1, 2, 3], because b = a made a copy
[1, 2, 3], because append returns a new list
questions.explain: Assignment binds a name to an existing object; it never copies. After b = a both names refer to one list, and append mutates that list in place. Use a.copy(), list(a) or a[:] when you need an independent shallow copy.
explain_choice: The ints are immutable, but the list holding them is not, and that is what changed.
Assignment copies a reference, not the list, so both names see every change.
append mutates in place and returns None; no second list is created.

questions.prompt: Which statement about tuples is true?
choices: A tuple's items can be reassigned but not appended to
Any tuple can be a dict key, since tuples are immutable
A tuple is hashable only if every item in it is
Putting a list inside a tuple raises TypeError
questions.explain: A tuple fixes which objects it refers to, not the state of those objects. Its hash is built from its items' hashes, so ([1], 2) can be created but hashing it raises TypeError on the list. Immutable and hashable are related but separate properties.
explain_choice: Item assignment such as t[0] = 1 raises TypeError; a tuple's slots are fixed.
Immutability is not enough: a tuple containing a list cannot be hashed, so it cannot be a key.
A tuple may hold any object; the error only appears when you try to hash it.

questions.prompt: When is a set the better choice than a list?
choices: When memory is tight, as sets are smaller than lists
When items are lists that must stay unique
Whenever items are sorted, as sets keep them in order
Frequent `in` checks or de-duplication, order not needed
questions.explain: A set is a hash table: `x in s` hashes x and checks one slot, O(1) on average, where a list compares item by item, O(n). The price is that items must be hashable, there is no position or order, and a set uses more memory per item than a list.
explain_choice: A set's spare hash slots make it larger than a list of the same items.
Lists are unhashable, so they cannot go into a set at all; convert them to tuples first.
A set has no defined order; iterating it will not give sorted or insertion order.

questions.prompt: What does `except Exception: pass` cost you?
choices: It hides real bugs, like a typo's NameError
It slows the try block even when nothing fails
Little: it catches errors raised by your own code
It also swallows Ctrl+C and calls to sys.exit()
questions.explain: Exception is the base of nearly every runtime error, including the NameError, AttributeError and TypeError your own typos raise, so the handler turns bugs into silent wrong results. KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit derive from BaseException and still escape, and since 3.11 a try that raises nothing costs almost nothing. Catch the specific exception you expect.
explain_choice: Since 3.11 entering a try block is essentially free; the cost is hidden bugs, not speed.
It catches errors from anything called inside the try, library code and your own bugs alike.
KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit derive from BaseException, not Exception, so they escape this handler.

questions.prompt: Why prefer `pathlib.Path` over string paths?
choices: It checks that the path exists when you create it
open() and os functions no longer accept plain strings
It makes file reads faster than open() on a string
Joining and parsing follow the host OS's path rules
questions.explain: A Path is a value object whose / operator, .name, .suffix and .parent apply the platform's separator and drive rules, so no string surgery can go wrong on Windows. Creating one does not touch the disk, and open() and os functions accept strings and Paths alike because Path implements os.PathLike.
explain_choice: Path() is pure string handling; call .exists() or .resolve(strict=True) to touch the disk.
Strings still work everywhere; Path is accepted because it implements os.PathLike.
Reading goes through the same open() either way; Path changes how paths are built, not I/O speed.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between `is` and `==`?
choices: is compares type as well as value; == compares value
is checks for one object; == calls __eq__ on values
is compares values faster, so suits small integers
Equal strings are one object, so is and == agree
questions.explain: `a is b` asks whether both names point at the same object, which CPython checks by address; `a == b` calls a.__eq__(b). Small ints and some strings happen to be cached, so `is` can seem to work and then fail on other values. Keep `is` for singletons such as None.
explain_choice: Two distinct lists of the same type and contents are == but not `is`; identity is not a stricter equality.
Small ints being cached is an implementation detail; 1000 is 1000 can be False for computed values.
Only some strings are interned; two equal strings built at runtime are usually separate objects.

questions.prompt: A dict key must be:
choices: Unique by identity, not by equality
A str or int, as in JSON object keys
Hashable, with a hash consistent with ==
Immutable, so a tuple of lists will work
questions.explain: A dict finds a key by hashing it to a slot, then confirming the match with ==. So a key needs __hash__, and objects that compare equal must hash equal or lookups miss. A tuple holding a list is immutable yet unhashable, and 1 and 1.0 are the same key because they are equal and hash alike.
explain_choice: Keys are matched by equality after hashing, so two equal but distinct strings are one key.
Any hashable object works: tuples, frozensets, floats, None and your own classes.
Immutability is not the test; a tuple containing a list is immutable but cannot be hashed.

questions.prompt: What does a good unit test assert?
choices: The whole workflow end to end, so it catches more at once
One behaviour, including its awkward edge cases
That the function completes without raising
Every line of the function, for 100% coverage
questions.explain: A test earns its keep by failing for exactly one reason, so a red test names what broke. Running without error asserts nothing about the output, coverage counts executed lines rather than checked results, and a broad test that fails could mean any of a dozen things.
explain_choice: End-to-end tests have their place, but when one fails it does not tell you which part broke.
A function can run cleanly and return the wrong answer; the test must check the result.
Coverage says which lines ran, not whether their results were checked.

questions.prompt: One function reads a file, parses it and emails a report. What is the main design problem?
choices: It needs type hints before it can be tested
It should be a class, since it keeps state
Its parsing cannot be tested without real I/O
It should catch every error so the email goes
questions.explain: When decision logic sits between two side effects, every test has to fake a file system and a mail server just to check parsing. Pull the parse into a pure function that takes text and returns data, keep reading and sending at the edges, and the core becomes a one-line test.
explain_choice: Hints help a checker, but the function would still need a file and a mail server to test.
Wrapping the same tangle in a class keeps the I/O and logic just as entangled.
Swallowing errors to force a send hides failures; the fix is separating logic from I/O.

questions.prompt: A module ends with `if __name__ == "__main__": main()`. What does the guard achieve?
choices: It stops the module from being imported twice
It is required for python file.py to run the file at all
It makes main() run first, before other top-level code
main() runs when executed as a script, not when imported
questions.explain: Python sets a module's __name__ to its import name, but to '__main__' for the file started with python file.py or python -m. The guard therefore separates being run from being imported, so tests can import the functions without launching the program. Repeat imports are prevented by the sys.modules cache, a separate mechanism.
explain_choice: Import caching in sys.modules prevents repeat imports; the guard has nothing to do with it.
A file runs top to bottom without any guard; the guard only matters when the file is imported.
Top-level code runs in order; the guard only decides whether main() runs, and it runs last.

questions.prompt: Your script is named `random.py`, and a module it uses runs `import random`. What happens?
choices: Your file wins: the script's folder is first on sys.path
The stdlib module wins, as built-ins are searched first
Whichever of the two files was modified most recently
Python raises ImportError over the ambiguous name
questions.explain: import walks sys.path in order and takes the first match, and sys.path[0] is the running script's directory. Only built-in and frozen modules, such as sys, are found before that; random is an ordinary .py file in the stdlib, so yours shadows it. Since 3.13 the resulting error message points out the likely shadowing.
explain_choice: Only built-in and frozen modules come first; random is a normal stdlib file, found after your folder.
Modification times play no part; the order of sys.path decides.
The search stops at the first match, so there is never an ambiguity to report.

questions.prompt: Why define `class ConfigError(Exception)` instead of raising ValueError everywhere?
choices: It stops the error being caught by `except Exception`
Callers can catch it without catching unrelated errors
Custom exceptions print clearer tracebacks than built-ins
Library code should not raise built-in exception types
questions.explain: except matches by class, subclasses included. A ValueError can come from any int() call deep in your stack, so `except ValueError` may hide a bug, while `except ConfigError` catches only what you raised. It still derives from Exception, so broad handlers see it, and `raise ConfigError(...) from err` keeps the original cause.
explain_choice: A subclass of Exception is still caught by `except Exception`; that is how subclass matching works.
Tracebacks look the same for every exception class; the gain is in how precisely callers can catch it.
Raising ValueError or TypeError for bad arguments is normal; the point is distinguishing your own failures.

questions.prompt: `json.loads(json.dumps({1: 'a'}))` returns what?
choices: {'1': 'a'}, since JSON object keys are strings
[[1, 'a']], since dict items become pairs
A TypeError, since dumps rejects int keys
{1: 'a'}, since the round trip is lossless
questions.explain: JSON objects only allow string keys, so dumps converts int, float, bool and None keys to strings, and loads has no record that they were ever anything else. Tuples come back as lists for the same reason. Convert keys back yourself, or store the data as a list of records.
explain_choice: A dict becomes a JSON object, with its keys turned into strings, not a list of pairs.
dumps accepts int, float, bool and None keys and converts them to strings; other key types raise TypeError.
JSON has fewer types than Python, so int keys and tuples do not survive the round trip.

questions.prompt: What does argparse give you over reading sys.argv by hand?
choices: Protection from shell injection in the arguments
Access to arguments that sys.argv does not receive
Arguments already split on spaces, unlike sys.argv
Type conversion, --help and usage errors, for free
questions.explain: sys.argv is already a list of strings split by the shell; you would still validate, convert and document them yourself. argparse declares each argument once and derives parsing, type conversion, defaults, the --help text, and on bad input a usage message with exit status 2.
explain_choice: Arguments reach Python as plain strings with no shell involved; argparse adds no escaping.
argparse reads sys.argv[1:] by default, so it sees exactly the same arguments.
The shell or the Windows runtime has already split the command line before sys.argv exists.

questions.prompt: A script runs nightly from a scheduler. Why use logging rather than print?
choices: print writes to the console, not to files
logging.info() shows by default, so nothing is missed
Records carry level, time and source, sent where you say
logging is faster, since print flushes after every call
questions.explain: A log record carries a level, timestamp, logger name and optional traceback, and handlers route it to files, rotation or syslog without touching the calling code. Levels let you turn detail up during an incident. The root logger's default level is WARNING, so info() stays silent until you call basicConfig or add a handler.
explain_choice: print(..., file=f) writes anywhere; what print lacks is levels, timestamps and central routing.
The root logger defaults to WARNING, so info() messages are dropped until you configure it.
print flushes per line only on an interactive terminal; the case for logging is structure and routing, not speed.

questions.prompt: What does pytest's `tmp_path` fixture give each test?
choices: The system temp folder, shared by all tests
A fresh, empty directory as a pathlib.Path
An in-memory filesystem that avoids the disk
A path string deleted as soon as the test ends
questions.explain: Each test that requests tmp_path gets its own new directory under a per-session base, so tests cannot see each other's files. It is a real directory on disk, handed over as a Path. pytest keeps the directories from the last three runs for inspection rather than deleting them straight away.
explain_choice: Each test gets a unique subdirectory, so files from one test cannot leak into another.
It is a real directory on disk, so code under test uses the ordinary file APIs.
It is a Path object, not a string, and pytest keeps recent runs' directories for inspection.

questions.prompt: `@dataclass class Cart: items: list = []`. What happens?
choices: Each Cart gets its own copy of the empty list
Every Cart shares one list, like a mutable default argument
A TypeError when the first Cart is created
ValueError when the class is built; use default_factory
questions.explain: The dataclass decorator refuses list, dict and set defaults, and since 3.11 any unhashable default, because the generated __init__ would share one object across instances. It raises ValueError while building the class, before any instance exists. field(default_factory=list) calls list() once per instance instead.
explain_choice: Nothing is copied automatically; a fresh list per instance needs field(default_factory=list).
That is the bug the decorator guards against; it rejects the default before it can be shared.
The check runs when @dataclass processes the class, so the error comes before any instance is made.

quizzes.name: Python engineering
quizzes.desc: Protocols, the object model, and laziness.

questions.prompt: What does a generator give you that a list doesn't?
choices: A result you can loop over as often as you like
Access to any item without computing the rest
Faster iteration, because nothing is stored
Items made on demand, so memory stays flat
questions.explain: A generator suspends its frame after each yield and resumes on the next request, so it holds one item's worth of state whatever the input size. The same design means no len(), no indexing and a single pass; iterating a list already in memory is usually no slower, and often faster.
explain_choice: A generator is single-pass; once exhausted it yields nothing more.
A generator has no index; reaching item n means producing the n items before it.
Resuming a frame per item has overhead; a generator saves memory, not iteration time.

questions.prompt: After you fully consume a generator, iterating it again yields:
choices: Nothing: the loop ends at once
StopIteration raised into your loop
The same items, from the start
The last item, which it keeps cached
questions.explain: A generator is its own iterator: once its frame has returned, every next() raises StopIteration immediately, which a for loop treats as the normal end. Nothing restarts it; call the generator function again for a fresh one, or store the results in a list if you need two passes.
explain_choice: StopIteration is raised, but the for loop consumes it as its end signal, so no error reaches you.
A generator does not rewind; only calling the generator function again starts a new one.
A finished generator keeps no values; its frame has been released.

questions.prompt: Why use `functools.wraps` in a decorator?
choices: It forwards *args and **kwargs to the function
It copies __name__, __doc__, sets __wrapped__
It lets the decorator work on methods as well
It caches the wrapper so decoration runs once
questions.explain: The wrapper is a new function object, so without help its name and docstring are the wrapper's own. wraps copies __module__, __name__, __qualname__, __doc__ and __dict__ and sets __wrapped__, so help(), logging and inspect.signature describe the original. Forwarding arguments is still the wrapper body's job.
explain_choice: Forwarding is done by your wrapper's own *args, **kwargs; wraps only copies metadata.
Plain function decorators already work on methods through the descriptor protocol, with or without wraps.
wraps does no caching; decoration runs once per def anyway, and functools.cache is the caching tool.

questions.prompt: What does returning True from `__exit__` do?
choices: Re-raises the exception once clean-up has run
Keeps the resource from __enter__ open afterwards
Suppresses the exception raised in the with block
Marks clean-up as done; errors still propagate
questions.explain: When the block raises, Python calls __exit__(type, value, traceback) and checks the result: a true value means handled, so execution continues after the with statement. Returning None, the usual case, lets the exception carry on. If the block did not raise, the return value is ignored.
explain_choice: Re-raising is what a falsy return does; True tells Python the exception has been handled.
The return value says nothing about the resource; __exit__'s own code decides whether to close it.
The return value is not a status report; a true value swallows the exception.

questions.prompt: `typing.Protocol` lets you:
choices: Enforce at runtime that arguments have the right types
Declare an interface classes must inherit to satisfy
Describe a network wire format for serialising objects
Accept any class with matching methods, no inheritance
questions.explain: A checker compares a class's attributes and method signatures with the Protocol's members, so any matching class satisfies it without naming it: duck typing that is checked statically. At runtime nothing is enforced unless you add @runtime_checkable, and even then isinstance only checks that the names exist.
explain_choice: Protocols are for static checkers; the interpreter does not check argument types at call time.
Requiring inheritance is nominal typing, as with abc.ABC; Protocol matches by structure instead.
The name is about object protocols such as iteration, not network protocols or serialisation.

questions.prompt: Which of these is genuinely lazy?
choices: `[x*2 for x in data]`
`(x*2 for x in data)`
`list(x*2 for x in data)`
`{x*2 for x in data}`
questions.explain: Parentheses around a comprehension make a generator expression, which computes nothing until iterated. Square and curly brackets run the whole loop immediately and store every result, and wrapping a generator in list() consumes it on the spot, so laziness ends at the first eager call.
explain_choice: Square brackets build the complete list in memory before the expression finishes.
The inner part is lazy, but list() iterates it to the end straight away.
Curly brackets build a set eagerly, computing and hashing every item at once.

questions.prompt: Two objects compare equal but have different hashes. What breaks?
choices: Hashing the second one raises TypeError
Sorting, which orders items by their hash
Sets and dicts keep both or miss lookups
Nothing, as dicts compare keys with == alone
questions.explain: Dicts and sets look in the slot chosen by the hash and only then compare with ==. Equal objects with different hashes land in different slots, so a set keeps both and a lookup with an equal key misses. That is why defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None until you write a matching one.
explain_choice: Both objects hash without complaint; the failure is silent, in lookups and de-duplication.
Sorting uses __lt__ and never looks at hashes.
== is only consulted after the hash picks a slot, so mismatched hashes mean == is never reached.

questions.prompt: `itertools.islice` is preferable to slicing when:
choices: The source is an iterator, e.g. a generator or file
You want the result reversed with a negative step
The list is huge, since a[:10] copies all of it
You need a copy independent of the original
questions.explain: Slicing calls __getitem__, which generators and files lack. islice just calls next(), dropping or yielding items, so it works on any iterable without materialising it, but it cannot go backwards and rejects negative values. On a list, a[:10] already copies only ten references.
explain_choice: islice rejects negative start, stop and step because an iterator cannot look back.
a[:10] copies ten references, not the whole list; slicing a list is already cheap.
An ordinary list slice is already a new, independent list.

questions.prompt: What does `yield from another_gen()` do?
choices: Yields each value; send() and throw() stop at this level
Collects the inner generator into a list, then yields it
Hands the inner generator object back to the caller
Delegates, forwarding send() and throw() and its return
questions.explain: `yield from sub` connects the caller straight to sub: every value sub yields passes out, every send() and throw() passes in, and when sub returns, its return value becomes the value of the yield from expression. A plain `for x in sub: yield x` passes values out but drops send, throw and the return value.
explain_choice: That is the behaviour of a plain for loop with yield; yield from forwards send() and throw().
Nothing is collected; values pass through one at a time, so it stays lazy.
It iterates the inner generator, yielding its items; the caller never sees the generator object.

questions.prompt: You want retry-with-backoff on twenty functions. Best tool?
choices: A base class whose __call__ retries subclass work
One try/except around main() that restarts it
A decorator with arguments, e.g. @retry(times=3)
A shared helper each function calls in a loop
questions.explain: Retrying is cross-cutting: it wraps a call without caring what the body does. A decorator factory takes the policy as arguments and returns a decorator, so each of the twenty functions gets one line and the loop exists once. Inheritance ties unrelated functions to a class, and a global handler restarts everything instead of the one failed call.
explain_choice: Turning twenty functions into subclasses couples unrelated code just to share a loop.
Restarting the whole program repeats work that succeeded and loses state; retry belongs at the call.
Each function would still carry its own loop around the helper, so the duplication remains.

questions.prompt: How does a `Protocol` differ from a PEP 695 type parameter such as `def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T`?
choices: They are two spellings of the same feature since Python 3.12
A Protocol constrains shape; T relates types in a signature
T is checked at runtime; a Protocol just by the checker
A Protocol needs subclassing; T accepts any type by shape
questions.explain: A Protocol is a structural type: any class with matching members satisfies it. A type parameter is a placeholder the checker solves at each call, so first([1, 2]) is typed int. They combine, as in def longest[T: Sized](xs: list[T]) -> T, where the bound limits T to Sized types. Neither is enforced at runtime.
explain_choice: PEP 695 added syntax for generics; Protocol, from PEP 544, is structural subtyping, a separate idea.
Neither is checked at runtime; both exist for static checkers.
Protocols match by structure without subclassing; T is a placeholder, not a structural check.

questions.prompt: What belongs in pyproject.toml?
choices: Test fixtures and sample data shared across tests
Build metadata, dependency ranges and tool settings
Runtime config such as database URLs and API keys
Exact pinned versions of every transitive dependency
questions.explain: The file is read by build frontends and tools, not by your running code: [build-system] says how to build, [project] declares name, version and dependency ranges, and [tool.*] tables hold Ruff, mypy and pytest settings. Resolved exact versions belong in the lockfile, and secrets in the environment.
explain_choice: Fixtures are code in conftest.py and test data lives in files; pyproject only configures pytest.
Runtime settings and secrets belong in the environment or a config file the app reads, never in build metadata.
Exact resolved versions, transitive ones included, are what a lockfile such as uv.lock records.

questions.prompt: `pip install -e .` does what?
choices: Installs a link to your source, so edits apply at once
Installs a frozen copy, so edits need a reinstall
Installs the dependencies but not the package itself
Installs the package together with its optional [dev] extras
questions.explain: An editable install puts a .pth entry or import hook in the environment that points imports at your source tree, so a changed .py file is picked up at the next import. Metadata is still captured at install time, so new dependencies or entry points in pyproject.toml need the install run again.
explain_choice: A frozen copy is what a normal install makes; -e is precisely the opposite.
The package itself is installed too, in editable form, along with its dependencies.
Extras are opt-in with brackets, as in pip install -e ".[dev]"; -e alone does not add them.

questions.prompt: A pytest fixture is for:
choices: A recorded sample output tests compare against
A mock that replaces network calls in tests
A helper that makes assertions for many tests
Setup and teardown that a test requests by name
questions.explain: pytest reads a test function's parameter names and calls the fixture functions with those names, running the code before yield as setup and the code after it as teardown. The scope argument decides how often it is rebuilt, so dependencies are explicit and each test gets a fresh one by default.
explain_choice: Comparing with stored output is snapshot testing; a fixture provides setup, not expected results.
A fixture can provide a mock, but mocking is one use, not what fixtures are.
Assertions belong in the test; a fixture supplies what the test needs to run.

questions.prompt: What does property-based testing (Hypothesis) add over example tests?
choices: It runs your example tests in parallel so they finish sooner
It proves a property holds for every possible input
Generated inputs, and failures shrunk to a minimal case
It infers expected outputs from the function's types
questions.explain: You state a property that must hold for all inputs, and Hypothesis draws many inputs from strategies, favouring nasty ones such as empty strings, huge ints and NaN. When one fails it shrinks it step by step to the simplest failing example and stores it for replay. It is a search, not a proof.
explain_choice: Hypothesis is about which inputs are tried, not how fast tests run.
It tries a finite sample, a hundred examples by default, so a passing run is evidence, not proof.
You write the property; Hypothesis generates inputs but cannot know what the right output is.

questions.prompt: 100% test coverage means:
choices: Every line ran at least once during the tests
Every branch and input combination was tested
The tests would catch any change in behaviour
Every function's result was checked by an assert
questions.explain: Line coverage records which lines executed, not what was asserted about them. A test that calls a function and checks nothing still reaches 100%, branch coverage is a separate measure, and a line that ran once with one input says nothing about the others. Mutation testing is how you check that tests notice changes.
explain_choice: Line coverage ignores which way each condition went; branch coverage is a separate, stricter measure.
Lines can run with no assertion on their result, so a changed behaviour can pass unnoticed.
Coverage tools record execution only; they cannot see whether a result was asserted.

questions.prompt: Why pin dependencies with a lockfile?
choices: It speeds up imports by pre-resolving modules
It blocks packages with known vulnerabilities
It stops dependencies from ever being upgraded
Every install resolves to the same exact versions
questions.explain: pyproject.toml declares ranges such as requests>=2.31, and a fresh resolve picks whatever is newest that day. A lockfile records the exact version and hash of every package, transitive ones included, so CI, a colleague and production install the same files. You upgrade on purpose, by relocking.
explain_choice: Locking affects what gets installed, not how Python imports it at runtime.
A lock pins whatever was resolved, vulnerable or not; scanning is a separate tool such as pip-audit.
You upgrade deliberately by relocking; the lock makes upgrades explicit, not impossible.

questions.prompt: A console-script entry point gives you:
choices: A compiled .exe that runs on machines without Python installed
A way to run the package with python -m mypkg
A command on PATH that calls a function in your package
A script file copied into site-packages at install
questions.explain: [project.scripts] maps a name to module:function. On install the installer writes a small launcher into the environment's bin or Scripts folder, which is on PATH while the environment is active; on Windows it is a tiny .exe that still starts that environment's Python. python -m relies on a __main__.py instead.
explain_choice: The Windows launcher is a small stub that starts the environment's Python; it is not a standalone build.
python -m mypkg runs mypkg/__main__.py; it needs no entry point at all.
The launcher goes into the environment's bin or Scripts folder, which is what puts it on PATH.

questions.prompt: Semantic versioning, at 1.4.2: you removed a public function. The next version is:
choices: A patch bump, to 1.4.3
A major bump, to 2.0.0
No bump until users report it
A minor bump, to 1.5.0
questions.explain: Semver encodes compatibility: MAJOR changes when code written against the old public API can break. Removing a function breaks every caller of it, however well the changelog explains it. Before 1.0.0 the spec promises nothing, which is why projects on 0.x often break things in a minor bump.
explain_choice: Patch is for backwards-compatible bug fixes; a removal can break callers.
The version describes the change you shipped, whether or not anyone has noticed yet.
Minor is for backwards-compatible additions; removing an API is incompatible.

questions.prompt: Average lookup cost in a hash table that resizes as it grows:
choices: O(1): the hash picks the slot directly
O(n): each key is compared until a match
O(n/b): n keys spread over b fixed buckets
O(log n): keys sit in sorted buckets
questions.explain: Hashing the key computes a slot index directly, and resizing keeps the ratio of keys to slots, the load factor, bounded, so the expected number of probes stays constant as n grows. Many colliding keys degrade a lookup to O(n), which is why hash quality matters.
explain_choice: Comparing every key is a linear scan; the hash lets you skip straight to one slot.
The bucket count is not fixed: resizing grows it with n, so n/b stays bounded by a constant.
Buckets are not kept sorted; O(log n) describes a balanced tree, not a hash table.

questions.prompt: Why is appending to a Python list amortised O(1)?
choices: Each append copies the list, but in fast C code
It over-allocates, so most appends need no copy
Lists are linked, so appending just adds a node
realloc grows the block in place, so nothing moves
questions.explain: When a list is full, CPython reallocates to roughly 1.125 times the needed size plus a small constant, so a copy of n pointers happens only after about n/8 cheap appends. Spreading that occasional O(n) copy over the appends it paid for gives O(1) each on average; one unlucky append is still O(n).
explain_choice: Copying on every append would be O(n) each, however fast the C; amortisation needs spare capacity.
A list is a contiguous array of pointers, which is why indexing is O(1).
The allocator often has to move the block; growth is cheap because spare slots make moves rare.

questions.prompt: You need the smallest item repeatedly while inserting. Use:
choices: A list kept sorted with bisect.insort
A set, calling min() on it each time
A binary heap managed with heapq
A dict mapping each item to its rank
questions.explain: A heap keeps a single invariant, each parent no larger than its children, so the minimum sits at index 0 and a push or pop repairs one root-to-leaf path in O(log n). A sorted list pays O(n) per insert to shift elements, and min() over a set scans everything each time.
explain_choice: bisect finds the spot in O(log n), but inserting shifts every later element, O(n) per insert.
min() over a set is an O(n) scan on every call; a set keeps no order at all.
Every insert can change many ranks, so keeping ranks current costs O(n).

questions.prompt: A linked list beats an array when:
choices: You want less memory per item than an array uses
You need to iterate over all items as fast as possible
You insert mid-list, searching for the spot each time
You splice at a node you already hold a reference to
questions.explain: Unlinking or inserting beside a node you already hold is O(1) pointer surgery, where an array must shift every later element. But reaching that node by position or value is an O(n) walk, and scattered nodes defeat CPU caches, so arrays win unless you really do hold the node.
explain_choice: Every node carries one or two pointers besides its value, so a linked list uses more memory per item.
Arrays iterate faster: contiguous memory is cache-friendly, while each node hop risks a cache miss.
Finding the spot is an O(n) walk, which cancels the O(1) splice; an array shift is usually faster.

questions.prompt: An unbalanced binary search tree degrades to O(n) lookups when:
choices: Lookups mostly hit keys near the leaves
Keys arrive in sorted order, with no rebalancing
It holds more keys than fit in the CPU cache at once
Keys are strings rather than integers
questions.explain: A BST's cost is its height. Inserting 1, 2, 3 and so on puts each new key in the right child of the last, so the tree becomes a linked list of height n. Self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees rotate on insert to keep the height O(log n).
explain_choice: In a balanced tree even leaves are O(log n) deep; the shape, not the access pattern, is the problem.
Cache misses slow each step by a constant factor; the step count still depends on height.
Any totally ordered key type works; comparing strings costs more per step but does not change the shape.

questions.prompt: A trie is the right choice for:
choices: Storing many strings in less memory than a set
Exact lookup of a word, faster than with a dict
Finding all words that start with a typed prefix
Range queries over numeric keys such as dates
questions.explain: A trie stores one character per edge, so all keys sharing a prefix share a path. Walking the prefix takes time proportional to its length, and everything below that node is the answer set. For exact lookup a dict is usually faster, and per-node overhead often makes a trie larger than a set of the same strings.
explain_choice: Each node carries a child map, so a Python trie usually uses more memory than a set of strings.
A dict hashes the whole key in one C loop and probes once; a trie follows one node per character.
Ordered numeric ranges suit a sorted array or B-tree; a trie organises keys by character prefix.

questions.prompt: Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix: pick a list when:
choices: The graph is sparse, with far fewer edges than V²
Edges carry weights, which a matrix has no room for
You must test whether u–v is an edge in O(1)
Most pairs of vertices are connected by an edge
questions.explain: A matrix allocates V² cells whether or not edges exist, and listing one vertex's neighbours scans a whole row. Adjacency lists store only the E edges that exist, O(V + E) memory, and iterate neighbours directly. The matrix wins for dense graphs and constant-time edge tests; weights fit in either.
explain_choice: A matrix stores a weight in each cell as easily as a 1, so weights do not decide it.
An O(1) edge test is the matrix's advantage; a list must scan the neighbours of u.
In a dense graph E approaches V², so the matrix costs little extra and gives O(1) edge tests.

questions.prompt: In CPython, `def f(): x = [1, 2, 3]`. Where does the list object live?
choices: On the C stack, and it is freed when f returns
On the heap, but passing x to g copies the list
On the stack, unless it grows too big for it
On the heap; x is a reference held in f's frame
questions.explain: Every Python object is a heap-allocated PyObject; a local name is a slot in the frame holding a pointer to it, and since 3.11 even those slots live in heap-allocated chunks rather than on the C stack. When f returns the slot is cleared and the refcount drops, so the list is freed only if nothing else still refers to it, which is how it can outlive the call.
explain_choice: That is C's model; in CPython the object is on the heap and reference counting, not the return, decides when it dies.
Passing an argument copies the reference, never the object, so g sees and can mutate the same list.
Size never decides placement in CPython; every object, however small, is allocated on the heap.

questions.prompt: Why does a deque beat a list for a FIFO queue in Python?
choices: popleft() is O(1); list.pop(0) shifts every item
deque stores items contiguously, so it caches better
Both pop from the front in O(1); deque uses less memory
deque indexes in O(1) at both ends and in the middle
questions.explain: A list is one contiguous array, so removing index 0 moves every remaining pointer down a slot, O(n). A deque is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks, so both ends are O(1) but indexing the middle walks blocks, O(n). A FIFO touches only the ends, which is exactly what a deque is built for.
explain_choice: A deque is a linked list of blocks; the list is the contiguous one.
list.pop(0) is O(n) because every later element shifts left one slot.
Indexing near the middle of a deque walks its blocks, O(n); only the ends are O(1).

questions.prompt: Why does a hash table resize once its load factor passes a threshold?
choices: Larger tables make computing each key's hash cheaper
Keys' hashes change as the table fills, so they need redoing
Fuller tables collide more, so probes per lookup climb
To keep keys in insertion order as the table grows
questions.explain: Load factor is keys divided by slots. As it rises, the chance that a new key's slot is taken rises too, and with open addressing probe sequences grow sharply near full. Resizing allocates more slots and reinserts every key, an O(n) step amortised over the inserts that led to it; CPython's dict resizes at about two-thirds full.
explain_choice: Hashing costs the same whatever the table size; resizing reduces collisions, not hashing work.
A key's hash never changes; only the slot it maps to changes when the table size does.
Insertion order in CPython's dict comes from a separate compact entries array, not from resizing.

questions.prompt: Two keys hash to the same slot. How does CPython's dict handle it?
choices: It rehashes every key using a different hash function
Open addressing: it probes other slots in a fixed order
The newer key overwrites the older one in that slot
Chaining: the slot holds a linked list of the entries
questions.explain: CPython uses open addressing: on a collision it derives a new index from the hash, mixing in higher bits through a perturbation value, and tries again until it finds the key or an empty slot. Java's HashMap chains instead. Either way both keys are kept, and a lookup confirms the right one by comparing hash and then ==.
explain_choice: The hash function stays the same; a collision just triggers probing for another slot.
Distinct keys are both kept; only a key equal to an existing one replaces its value.
Chaining is the textbook scheme and Java's; CPython's dict probes within its own table instead.

questions.prompt: An algorithm is Θ(n log n). What does that add over saying O(n log n)?
choices: Θ is the average case, while O is the worst case
Θ counts exact steps, while O drops the constants
Θ is the real-world cost, whereas O is just the theory
The bound is tight: it grows no faster and no slower
questions.explain: O is an upper bound, Ω a lower bound, and Θ means both hold, up to constant factors for large n. They describe a function, so each case can have its own: quicksort's worst case is Θ(n²) and its average Θ(n log n). Best, average and worst pick the input; O, Ω and Θ say how tightly you bound the cost.
explain_choice: Cases and bounds are separate ideas: you can give a Θ bound for the worst case or an O bound for the average.
Θ ignores constant factors exactly as O does; it adds a lower bound, not precision.
All three are asymptotic statements; none measures actual running time on real hardware.

questions.prompt: Summing ten million ints: an array and a linked list are both O(n). Why is the array far faster in practice?
choices: Array loops are O(n), but list walks are O(n log n)
Contiguous memory is read in cache lines and prefetched
Linked lists need an extra comparison at every node
Following each pointer costs the CPU a system call per node
questions.explain: Big O counts operations, not what each one costs. An array's elements sit side by side, so one cache-line fetch delivers several and the prefetcher streams the rest. Each list node can be anywhere in memory, so every pointer hop risks a cache miss costing on the order of a hundred cycles. Same complexity, very different constant.
explain_choice: Walking a list visits each node once, which is O(n), the same as the array.
Both loops check one end condition per element; the difference is memory access, not comparisons.
Dereferencing a pointer is an ordinary memory load; the cost is cache misses, not the kernel.

questions.prompt: A breadth-first search keeps its frontier in a stack instead of a queue. What changes?
choices: It explores depth-first, so shortest paths are lost
Nothing, as long as visited nodes are still marked
It finds the same shortest paths, just more slowly
It fails, as a stack loses track of unvisited nodes
questions.explain: BFS's guarantee comes from FIFO order: every node at distance d leaves the queue before any at d + 1, so a node is first reached by a shortest path. A LIFO stack always expands the newest node, diving down one branch first. Same loop, different container, different algorithm.
explain_choice: Marking visited nodes prevents repeats but does not restore the level-by-level order.
Without FIFO order a node can first be reached by a longer path, so the shortest-path guarantee goes.
Every pushed node is still expanded eventually; only the order changes.

questions.prompt: Which traversal of a binary search tree yields its keys in sorted order?
choices: Pre-order: node, left, right
Level-order: row by row from the root
Post-order: left, right, node
In-order: left, node, right
questions.explain: The BST invariant puts every smaller key in the left subtree and every larger one in the right. Visiting left, then the node, then right therefore emits all smaller keys, then the key, then all larger keys, recursively, which is sorted order. Pre-order is the one you use to copy a tree's shape.
explain_choice: Pre-order emits the root before any smaller key, so the output starts in the middle of the range.
Each row mixes keys from both subtrees, so level order follows depth, not key order.
Post-order emits a node after all its larger keys in the right subtree, so it is not sorted.

questions.prompt: After `heapq.heapify(xs)`, which statement is guaranteed?
choices: xs is fully sorted in ascending order
xs[-1] holds the largest, like a sorted list
xs[0] is the smallest, but the list is not sorted
Each level of the heap is sorted left to right
questions.explain: heapq maintains only the invariant xs[k] <= xs[2k+1] and xs[k] <= xs[2k+2]. That pins the minimum at index 0 and says nothing about siblings or the last slot. heapify establishes it in O(n), cheaper than the O(n log n) a full sort needs.
explain_choice: A heap is only partially ordered; sorted order would cost O(n log n), more than heapify's O(n).
The largest item can be in any leaf, not necessarily the last slot.
Siblings have no required order; only each parent-child pair is constrained.

questions.prompt: What does CPython's cyclic garbage collector do that reference counting cannot?
choices: Frees objects as soon as their refcount reaches zero
Frees groups of objects that refer only to each other
Compacts the heap by moving live objects together
Returns freed memory to the OS on every collection
questions.explain: Reference counting frees an object the moment its count hits zero, but two objects that point at each other never reach zero even when nothing else can reach them. The gc module periodically finds such unreachable cycles among container objects and breaks them. CPython never moves objects, which is why id() stays stable for an object's lifetime.
explain_choice: Freeing at zero is reference counting's job; the collector exists for the cycles it misses.
CPython does not move objects, so addresses and id() never change during an object's life.
Freed memory usually returns to CPython's own allocator pools, not straight to the OS.

questions.prompt: Why does a Python list of a million ints use far more memory than a C int array?
choices: Python keeps each int as a float, which is wider
The list reserves double its length at all times
Python stores each int as text, parsed when used
Each item is a pointer to a separate int object
questions.explain: A C int array stores raw 4-byte values side by side. A Python list stores 8-byte pointers, each to a full int object of about 28 bytes carrying a refcount, a type pointer and a size. Small ints from -5 to 256 are shared, but most values cost around 36 bytes where C spends 4; array.array and numpy store raw values instead.
explain_choice: int and float are separate types; a Python int is an arbitrary-precision integer object.
Over-allocation adds about an eighth, not double; the cost is a pointer plus an object per item.
Ints are stored as binary digits inside an object; parsing text happens only at int('...').

quizzes.name: Algorithms
quizzes.desc: Choosing the approach before writing code.

questions.prompt: Binary search over a Python list gives O(log n) lookups only when the list is:
choices: Free of duplicates, so each value sits at exactly one position
Stored as a linked list, so halves can be split off
Sorted by the search key, with fast access by index
Loaded into a set first, so membership is instant
questions.explain: Each step compares against the middle element and discards the half that cannot hold the target, which is only valid if order tells you which half that is. Jumping to the middle must also be cheap: on a linked list reaching the midpoint is itself O(n). Duplicates are fine, and `bisect_left` finds the first of them.
explain_choice: Duplicates do not break the halving argument; bisect_left and bisect_right return the first and last insertion points among equal values.
Splitting a linked list still means walking to its middle, which costs O(n) per step and destroys the logarithmic bound.
A set does answer membership in O(1) on average, but that is hashing, not binary search, and it keeps no order to search.

questions.prompt: Two nested loops, each running over the same n-element list, perform how much work?
choices: O(n²): the inner loop runs n times for each of n outer steps
O(2ⁿ): each extra element doubles the combinations checked
O(n log n): the inner loop gets shorter as the outer one advances
O(n): each loop is linear, and the two add up to 2n
questions.explain: Nesting multiplies rather than adds: every one of the n outer iterations pays for a full pass of the inner loop, n × n. Even a triangular inner loop (`for j in range(i)`) is n(n-1)/2 steps, which is still quadratic.
explain_choice: Exponential growth comes from enumerating subsets; two nested loops only enumerate pairs, of which there are n².
A shrinking inner loop gives n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2 steps, which is quadratic, not n log n.
Costs add only when loops run one after the other; nested loops multiply, because the inner loop repeats for every outer step.

questions.prompt: Memoization turns an exponential recursion into a polynomial one when the problem has:
choices: Large inputs, where caching every result saves memory
Deep recursion that keeps hitting Python's default recursion limit
Many base cases, which the cache can return instantly
Overlapping subproblems that the recursion keeps recomputing
questions.explain: A cache only saves work if the same call is made again. Naive Fibonacci calls fib(n-2) from two places, and so on down, so the call tree is exponential but has only n distinct nodes; caching each result once collapses the tree to those n calls. Merge sort, whose subproblems never repeat, gains nothing from a cache.
explain_choice: Memoization trades memory for time; it stores one result per distinct subproblem, so it uses more memory, not less.
A cache does nothing for depth: the first call to fib(5000) still recurses 5000 frames deep before anything is cached.
Base cases are already cheap to compute; the saving comes from not repeating large subproblems.

questions.prompt: Choose BFS over DFS when you need:
choices: A topological order of tasks with dependencies
The fewest-edges path between two nodes in an unweighted graph
The lowest memory use when exploring a very wide, shallow graph
To detect whether a directed graph contains a cycle
questions.explain: BFS visits nodes in rings of increasing distance from the start, so the first time it reaches a node it has done so along a path with the fewest possible edges. DFS reaches nodes along whatever path it happened to explore first. On a wide graph BFS's queue holds a whole frontier, which is the opposite of small.
explain_choice: The classic topological sort is DFS finishing order reversed; Kahn's algorithm is queue-based, but it processes in-degree zero nodes, not shortest paths.
On a wide, shallow graph BFS holds an entire level in its queue, while DFS holds only the current path, so DFS is the lighter one.
Directed cycle detection is usually DFS with a 'currently on the stack' colour; BFS has no natural notion of a back edge.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm can return wrong distances when the graph has:
choices: Negative edge weights
Directed, one-way edges
Edges with weight zero
Cycles of any length
questions.explain: Dijkstra settles the closest unsettled node and never revisits it, which is sound only if no later path can be shorter, and that holds only if adding an edge can never reduce a distance. A negative edge breaks exactly that. Zero-weight edges, cycles and directed edges are all handled correctly; with negative edges use Bellman-Ford.
explain_choice: Dijkstra is naturally defined on directed graphs; an undirected edge is just two directed ones.
A zero-weight edge cannot make a settled distance smaller, so the greedy step stays correct.
Cycles with non-negative weights never shorten a path, so Dijkstra handles them; only negative weights invalidate its settle-once rule.

questions.prompt: When can you trust a greedy algorithm to give the optimal answer?
choices: When the input has been sorted by the value you pick greedily
When an exchange argument proves each local choice is safe
When no dynamic-programming solution to the problem is known
When it passes every test case you wrote, edge cases included
questions.explain: Greedy commits to a choice and never reconsiders it, so correctness has to come from a proof such as an exchange argument: take any optimal solution, swap in the greedy choice, and show it is no worse. Coin change with denominations 1, 3 and 4 shows the risk; greedy pays 6 as 4+1+1 when 3+3 uses fewer coins.
explain_choice: Sorting is how many greedy algorithms start, but sorted input does not make a wrong greedy rule correct.
Whether a DP solution exists says nothing about whether the greedy choice is safe; many problems have both.
Tests sample a few inputs; greedy failures often need a specific counterexample, like coins {1, 3, 4} for 6, that a hand-written suite misses.

questions.prompt: What does `list.sort()` (and `sorted()`) use in CPython 3.11 and later?
choices: Introsort: quicksort that falls back to heapsort on bad pivots, so unstable
Quicksort with median-of-three pivots, so O(n²) in the worst case
Heapsort, which sorts in place and so needs no extra memory at all
Timsort, a stable adaptive merge sort, with the powersort merge policy
questions.explain: CPython finds already-ordered runs in the data and merges them, which makes it O(n) on sorted or nearly sorted input and O(n log n) in the worst case, using up to n/2 extra slots for merging. Since 3.11 the choice of which runs to merge follows the powersort policy, which has provably near-optimal merge costs. It is stable: equal keys keep their input order, which is what lets you sort by a secondary key first and then by the primary one.
explain_choice: Introsort is what C++ std::sort typically uses; Python chose a stable algorithm, so equal keys never swap places.
Quicksort is not what Python uses; its sort is a merge sort whose worst case is O(n log n).
Heapsort is in place but unstable and cannot exploit existing order; Python's sort does use extra memory for merging.

questions.prompt: Faced with an unfamiliar problem, what is the most useful first step?
choices: Write the full test suite before any solution code
Pick the data structure, then design the algorithm
Write a brute-force solution and state its complexity
Search for the known optimal algorithm before writing any code
questions.explain: A correct slow solution does three jobs: it proves you understand the problem, it becomes an oracle to compare a faster version against on random inputs, and its complexity tells you exactly what you need to beat. Choosing a structure or searching first often solves a problem you have not yet pinned down.
explain_choice: Tests matter, but without a working reference you cannot generate expected outputs for random cases; brute force supplies that oracle.
The right structure usually falls out of the brute force's bottleneck; choosing it first is guessing.
Searching first skips the understanding the phase is building, and on a truly new problem there may be nothing to find.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes backtracking from plain brute-force enumeration?
choices: Using recursion, where brute force uses loops over every candidate
Cutting off a partial solution once it can't lead to a valid answer
Keeping an explicit stack of choices rather than using the call stack
Running in polynomial time, where brute force is exponential
questions.explain: Both explore the same tree of choices. Backtracking checks constraints on each partial solution and cuts off the whole subtree below one that already fails, so in N-queens it never places a fifth queen on a board whose first four already attack each other. Its worst case is often still exponential; pruning changes how much of the tree you actually visit.
explain_choice: Brute force can be written recursively too; recursion is a style, and the defining step is the pruning.
An explicit stack is an implementation choice that either approach can use.
Backtracking is usually still exponential in the worst case; pruning shrinks the search in practice, it does not change the complexity class in general.

questions.prompt: You need the 10 largest scores from a stream of a million. Which approach is cheapest in time and memory?
choices: Keep a 10-item min-heap; replace its root when a bigger score arrives
Call max() ten times on the list, removing each winner
Keep a 10-item max-heap, so the ten largest scores always sit at the top
Collect all million, sort them, and take the last ten
questions.explain: A min-heap of size k keeps its smallest kept score at the root, so each new score needs one comparison to reject it, or an O(log k) replace when it beats the root. That is O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, and it is what `heapq.nlargest(10, stream)` does. Sorting needs every score in memory and O(n log n) time.
explain_choice: Each max() and remove is a full O(n) pass over a list you had to store entirely, so ten of them cost more than one heap pass.
A max-heap puts the largest at the root, but to decide whether a new score belongs you need the smallest of the ten, which a max-heap buries.
It gives the right answer but holds a million scores and does O(n log n) work to keep ten.

questions.prompt: To find the smallest ship capacity that moves all packages within D days, you binary-search the capacity. What makes that valid?
choices: The package weights must be sorted before searching
It finds a local minimum, which is close enough here
Capacities are integers, and integer ranges can be halved
If a capacity works, every larger capacity also works
questions.explain: Binary search needs a predicate that flips once from false to true across the range. Here 'can ship in D days with capacity C' is monotonic: more capacity never makes it harder. So you test the middle capacity with a greedy O(n) simulation and discard the half that cannot contain the smallest working value. The packages stay in their given order.
explain_choice: The packages must ship in their given order, so sorting them changes the problem; the searched space is the capacity, not the list.
With a monotonic predicate, binary search finds the exact boundary, not an approximate or local answer.
Integers are necessary for a clean range, but halving only finds the answer if the feasibility test is monotonic over that range.

questions.prompt: A recursive DFS over a 100,000-node chain raises RecursionError. What is the durable fix?
choices: Make the recursive call the last line so Python drops the frame
Raise sys.setrecursionlimit() to 200,000 and move on
Rewrite it with an explicit stack kept in a list
Add @functools.cache so the repeated calls go away
questions.explain: The recursion limit (1000 by default) guards against running out of stack, and each recursive call adds a frame. An explicit stack moves the pending work into an ordinary list, whose size is limited only by memory, and the iteration visits the same nodes. CPython does no tail-call elimination, so the call's position changes nothing.
explain_choice: CPython does not eliminate tail calls; the caller's frame stays alive whatever line the call is on.
It can get this input through, but the next larger graph fails again, and very deep recursion can still crash the interpreter instead of raising cleanly.
A DFS visits each node once, so there are no repeated calls to cache, and a cache never reduces recursion depth.

quizzes.name: Linux & systems
quizzes.desc: The environment your code actually runs in.

questions.prompt: A script works in your terminal but fails when cron runs it. What is the most likely cause?
choices: cron kills any job that writes output to stdout
cron uses a minimal environment: short PATH, no profile, different cwd
cron uses the system Python rather than the one your shell finds
cron runs jobs as root, which the script's files don't allow
questions.explain: Your interactive shell sources ~/.bashrc or ~/.profile, which set PATH, activate tools and export variables. cron starts jobs with a tiny environment (often PATH=/usr/bin:/bin), in your home directory, without reading those files. So commands and relative paths that resolve in your terminal do not resolve under cron. Use absolute paths and set what you need in the crontab or the script.
explain_choice: cron does not kill jobs for writing output; it mails or discards it, depending on MAILTO.
cron finds whichever python is first on its short PATH; the real issue is that PATH, not a fixed rule about system Python.
A user's crontab runs as that user, not root; permission errors are possible but are not the usual cause.

questions.prompt: A command exits with status 0. What does that mean?
choices: It was killed by a signal before it could set its own status
It failed, since 0 means false in C and most other languages
It ran but produced no output on stdout or on stderr
It reported success; any non-zero status reports a failure
questions.explain: Unix inverts the boolean intuition so there is one way to succeed and many numbered ways to fail. `if cmd`, `&&`, `set -e` and CI runners all test for exactly 0. A shell reports a process killed by signal N as 128+N, so SIGKILL shows up as 137.
explain_choice: A signal death is reported by the shell as 128 plus the signal number, such as 137 for SIGKILL, never 0.
Exit statuses are not booleans: 0 is the single success value, and the 255 non-zero values are room for distinct failure codes.
Output and status are independent; a successful command can print a lot, and a silent one can fail.

questions.prompt: In `cmd > out.log 2>&1`, what does `2>&1` do?
choices: Copies stderr into a second file named '1'
Sends stdout into stderr, so both go to the terminal
Points stderr at whatever stdout points to at that moment
Links the two streams so any later redirect moves both of them
questions.explain: Redirections are applied left to right, and `2>&1` duplicates file descriptor 1 onto descriptor 2 as it is right then. After `> out.log`, descriptor 1 is the file, so stderr goes there too. In `2>&1 > out.log` stderr is copied from the terminal before stdout moves, so errors still reach the screen.
explain_choice: `2>1` would write to a file named 1; the ampersand marks the target as a file descriptor.
That is `1>&2`; the number on the left is the descriptor being redirected, here 2 (stderr).
It is a one-off copy, not a link: redirecting stdout afterwards leaves stderr where it was.

questions.prompt: `ps` shows a process in state Z (zombie). What is it?
choices: A process that has exited but whose parent hasn't read its status
A process that ignored SIGTERM and so keeps running
A process whose parent died, so init has adopted it
A process stuck in uninterruptible disk I/O, so it ignores every signal
questions.explain: When a process exits, the kernel keeps a small entry holding its exit status until the parent collects it with wait(). Until then it uses no CPU or memory beyond that slot, and kill cannot remove it because it is already dead. Fix the parent so it reaps, or end the parent: init adopts the zombie and reaps it.
explain_choice: A process that ignores SIGTERM is alive and running; a zombie has exited and cannot be signalled at all.
That is an orphan: it is still running, and init or a subreaper adopts it. A zombie has already exited.
That is state D; it is alive and waiting on I/O, whereas a zombie has finished.

questions.prompt: You `rm` a 20 GB log, but `df` shows no space freed. Why?
choices: A running process still has the file open
rm on Linux moves files to a trash directory
The page cache holds the data until it is dropped
The journal keeps the blocks until the next reboot
questions.explain: rm removes a name from a directory. The inode and its blocks are freed only when the link count reaches zero and no process has the file open. A logger still writing to it keeps the space in use; `lsof +L1` lists such deleted-but-open files. Restarting the process, or truncating through /proc/<pid>/fd, releases the space.
explain_choice: Command-line rm unlinks directly; a trash folder is a desktop-environment feature.
Cached pages of a deleted file are discarded with it; the page cache does not keep disk blocks allocated.
The journal records metadata changes and does not pin a deleted file's data until reboot.

questions.prompt: How do SIGTERM and SIGKILL differ?
choices: TERM goes to the whole process group; KILL to a single PID
KILL runs the process's atexit handlers first; TERM skips them
Both can be caught, but KILL gives the handler only five seconds to finish
TERM can be handled; KILL can never be caught, blocked or ignored
questions.explain: SIGTERM is a request: a program can install a handler to finish in-flight work, flush and exit. SIGKILL is handled by the kernel, which ends the process without running any of its code. Python installs no SIGTERM handler by default, so an unhandled TERM also skips `finally` blocks and atexit; add one with `signal.signal` if you need cleanup.
explain_choice: Which processes receive a signal depends on the PID you pass to kill (a negative one means a group), not on the signal.
KILL never runs any user code, atexit included; the process simply stops.
The grace period you may be thinking of is a tool's own policy, such as `docker stop` sending TERM then KILL; the signal itself cannot be caught.

questions.prompt: What does `set -euo pipefail` at the top of a bash script give you?
choices: Echo every command before it runs, which makes failures easy to trace
Exit on a failing command, error on unset variables, fail on any pipe stage
Run the script in POSIX mode so it works under sh as well as bash
Stop on every failure anywhere, including inside if and while tests
questions.explain: By default bash carries on after a failing command, expands an unset variable to an empty string, and takes a pipeline's status from its last stage only. So `rm -rf "$DIR/"` with DIR unset targets `/`, and `curl ... | tee` hides a failed download. The three options turn each of these into an early exit. set -e has deliberate exceptions: it does not fire for commands tested by if, while, && or ||.
explain_choice: Echoing commands is `set -x`, a separate debugging option.
These are bash options; `pipefail` did not appear in POSIX until 2024 and is missing from many sh implementations.
set -e is suspended inside conditions and before && or ||, so failures there do not stop the script.

questions.prompt: After `chmod 644 notes.txt`, who can do what?
choices: Everyone reads; only the owner can execute it
Owner and group read and write; everyone else can only read
Owner reads and writes; group and others read only
Owner reads, writes and executes; others read only
questions.explain: Each octal digit is a sum of read (4), write (2) and execute (1), in the order owner, group, others. 6 is 4+2, read and write; 4 is read. None of the digits includes 1, so nobody can execute it; a script usually wants 755.
explain_choice: No digit includes the execute bit (1), and the owner's 6 grants write.
Group read-write would make the middle digit 6; this describes 664.
Execute adds 1, so read-write-execute is 7; this describes 744.

questions.prompt: `p = Popen(cmd, stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE)` followed by `p.wait()` hangs on a command that prints a lot. Why?
choices: wait() without a timeout argument blocks forever on every command
The pipe's buffer fills, the child blocks writing, and nobody reads it
With both streams piped, the child deadlocks writing to itself
Popen keeps all output in Python memory until the process runs out
questions.explain: A pipe holds only a small kernel buffer, 64 KiB by default on Linux. Once it is full the child's next write blocks until someone reads, but the parent is sitting in wait() and reads nothing, so each waits for the other. `communicate()` (or `subprocess.run(..., capture_output=True)`) reads both pipes while waiting; for gigabytes of output, stream it to a file or read it line by line instead.
explain_choice: wait() returns as soon as the child exits; it only hangs here because the child cannot exit while blocked on a full pipe.
The child writes to pipes the parent owns, not to itself; the deadlock is between the child's writes and the parent's missing reads.
Nothing is read into Python until you read the pipe; the output sits in a small kernel buffer, and that buffer filling is the problem.

questions.prompt: You run `ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 bastion`. In that command, which machine does `localhost` mean?
choices: Whichever host on the network first answers on port 5432
Your own machine, since that is where you typed the command
The bastion, since the far end of -L is resolved on the SSH server
The database host behind the bastion, which SSH finds for you
questions.explain: `-L local_port:host:host_port` opens local_port on your machine and, for each connection, asks the SSH server to connect onward to host:host_port. That host name is resolved from the server's point of view, so `localhost` is the bastion itself. To reach a database behind the bastion, name it: `-L 5433:db.internal:5432`.
explain_choice: The destination is one fixed host and port that the SSH server connects to; nothing is broadcast.
Only the listening side, 5433, is on your machine; the destination is looked up by the SSH server.
SSH connects to exactly the host you name; it does no discovery, so `localhost` here is the bastion.

questions.prompt: A script runs `for f in $(ls *.log); do rm $f; done`. What happens with a file named `app 1.log`?
choices: The unquoted expansion splits it into the words `app` and `1.log`
Nothing goes wrong, since ls hands each filename over intact
Quoting rm's argument is enough; the for loop handles spaces itself
