ls escapes the space, and rm then fails on the stray backslash
questions.explain: `$(...)` output undergoes word splitting on spaces, tabs and newlines, and the unquoted `$f` is split again, so rm is asked to delete `app` and `1.log`, which may be different files. Glob directly and quote every expansion: `for f in ./*.log; do rm -- "$f"; done`. The `./` and `--` also stop a name starting with `-` being read as an option.
explain_choice: ls writes names as plain text, and the shell then splits that text on whitespace; the file boundaries are gone.
The loop over `$(ls)` has already split the name before rm sees it; both the loop source and `$f` need fixing.
The quoting you see from ls in a terminal is display-only; piped or captured output is unescaped, so nothing protects the space.

questions.prompt: On Linux, how do you find which process is listening on port 8080?
choices: Run `ping localhost:8080`, which reports the program that answers
Read /etc/services, which maps every port to its current process
Run `ps aux | grep 8080`, since ps lists each process's ports
Run `sudo ss -ltnp` and read the process for local port 8080
questions.explain: `ss -ltnp` lists listening (-l) TCP (-t) sockets with numeric ports (-n) and the owning process (-p). Without sudo it shows owners only for your own processes. `lsof -i :8080` answers the same question. The socket table lives in the kernel, so tools that read process arguments or static files cannot see it.
explain_choice: ping uses ICMP, which has no ports; it only tells you whether a host replies at all.
/etc/services is a static list of conventional port names, such as 80 for http; it knows nothing about running processes.
ps shows command lines, not sockets; grep only matches if 8080 happens to appear in an argument.

questions.prompt: An API call made with `requests.get(url)` sometimes hangs forever. The usual root cause is:
choices: No timeout was passed, and requests waits indefinitely by default
A DNS lookup failed, and resolution retries without end
The server is down, and a down server makes calls hang
TCP keepalive is switched off, so the client doesn't notice the dead socket
questions.explain: requests passes no timeout to the socket unless you give one, so a server that accepts the connection and then goes silent leaves the call blocked on a read forever. `timeout=(3.05, 30)` bounds the connect and each read. A refused connection or a failed DNS lookup raises an error; silence is what hangs.
explain_choice: A failed resolution raises an error after the resolver's own timeouts; it does not retry forever.
A down host usually gives connection refused or an OS connect timeout, which raises; the hang comes from a live peer that stops responding.
Keepalive probes start after hours by default and are not a request timeout; the fix is a timeout on the call itself.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is defined as idempotent but not safe?
choices: POST, provided the client sends exactly the same body again
GET, since reading twice gives the same result
PUT, which replaces the target with the body sent
PATCH, since it changes just the fields named
questions.explain: Idempotent means repeating the request leaves the server in the same state as sending it once; safe means it changes no state at all. PUT sets the resource to exactly the body, so a second identical PUT changes nothing more. GET is safe (and therefore idempotent). PATCH and POST are not idempotent in general: `{"op": "add", ...}` or 'append a comment' applied twice does twice the work.
explain_choice: Sending the same body again still asks the server to perform the action again, such as creating a second order.
GET is idempotent, but it is also safe, and the question asks for a method that changes state.
A patch can be a relative change, such as incrementing a counter, so repeating it changes the result; the spec does not require PATCH to be idempotent.

questions.prompt: A request through your load balancer returns 502. What does that tell you?
choices: Your request was malformed, and the server couldn't parse it
The proxy got an invalid response, or none, from the server behind it
The service is overloaded or in maintenance and refusing work
The server behind the proxy was too slow, so the proxy gave up waiting
questions.explain: 502 Bad Gateway is sent by an intermediary about its upstream: the backend crashed, closed the connection, or sent something that was not valid HTTP. The neighbouring codes separate the cases: 504 is the upstream timing out, 503 is 'unavailable right now', and 4xx codes blame the client. So a 502 sends you to the backend's logs, not your request.
explain_choice: A malformed request is a client error, 400, not a 5xx.
Overload or maintenance is 503 Service Unavailable, often with Retry-After.
An upstream that is too slow gives 504 Gateway Timeout.

questions.prompt: A client times out on `POST /payments` and retries with the same `Idempotency-Key` header. What must the server do for the retry to be safe?
choices: Nothing extra: sending a key header makes the POST idempotent
Hash the request body and drop any body it has already processed before
Reject the repeat with 409 so the client knows it was a duplicate
Store the key with the first result and replay that result for repeats
questions.explain: The client's timeout may have come after the payment was taken, so the retry must not charge again, and the client still needs to learn the result. The server records the key atomically with the result of the first request (the new payment's ID and status) and replays that response for the same key. Identical bodies are not duplicates in general: two genuine £10 payments look alike.
explain_choice: The header is only a promise from the client; the server's stored key-to-result mapping is what makes the retry harmless.
Two legitimate payments can have identical bodies; only a key the client chose per logical operation separates a retry from a new request.
A 409 leaves the client unsure whether its payment happened; replaying the original response tells it. 409 fits only a repeat that arrives while the first is still in progress.

questions.prompt: What does TCP guarantee to the application?
choices: Delivery within a bounded time, or an error at once
An ordered, reliable byte stream, with no message boundaries
Encryption of the bytes between the two endpoints
Each send() call arrives as exactly one matching recv() on the other side
questions.explain: TCP numbers every byte, retransmits what is lost and reorders what arrives early, so the receiver reads the same bytes in the same order. It says nothing about grouping: two sends can arrive in one recv, or one send across several. That is why every protocol on TCP needs framing, such as a length prefix or a delimiter. Latency is unbounded, and encryption is TLS's job.
explain_choice: Retransmission can take seconds or minutes; TCP promises eventual in-order delivery, not a time bound.
Plain TCP is readable on the wire; TLS adds encryption on top.
TCP is a stream: sends can be merged or split in transit, so a reader must frame messages itself.

questions.prompt: What does successful TLS certificate verification actually establish?
choices: The connection is encrypted, which without verification would be plaintext
The site is legitimate and safe to give your personal details to
The server has the key for a cert naming this host, from a CA you trust
The server's software has been audited for known vulnerabilities
questions.explain: Verification checks a chain of signatures from the server's certificate up to a root in your trust store, that the certificate names the host you asked for, and that it is in date; the handshake proves the server has the matching private key. That rules out a machine in the middle posing as the server. It says nothing about the owner's intentions, and any phishing domain can get a valid certificate.
explain_choice: The traffic is encrypted either way; turning verification off leaves it encrypted to whoever answered, which is what a man-in-the-middle attack exploits.
CAs check control of the domain, not honesty; phishing sites routinely have valid certificates.
A certificate says nothing about the server's patch level or code quality.

questions.prompt: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?
choices: So clients that failed together don't retry together
So each retry comes sooner and the call recovers faster
So retries slip under the server's rate limiter
So the request always succeeds if retried enough
questions.explain: When a service fails, all its clients see the error at roughly the same moment. With plain exponential backoff they then retry at the same moments, 1 s, 2 s, 4 s later, in synchronised waves that can knock the recovering service over again. Randomising each delay (for example, uniform between 0 and the backoff cap) spreads the retries into a steady trickle.
explain_choice: Jitter can lengthen or shorten an individual delay; its purpose is to spread load, not to speed up recovery.
Rate limiters count requests per client, however they are timed; jitter is about protecting the server, not evading it.
Retries cannot fix a permanent error such as a 400; backoff needs a cap on attempts or on total time.

questions.prompt: WebSockets beat periodic polling when:
choices: Each client sends one request and needs exactly one reply back
Responses should be cached by browsers and CDNs
Updates are rare, a few times a day at most
The server must push frequent updates with low delay
questions.explain: Polling asks 'anything new?' on a timer, so you choose between delay (a long interval) and wasted requests (a short one). A WebSocket keeps one connection open, and the server writes to it the moment something happens. That only pays off when updates are frequent enough to justify the held connection; rare updates are cheaper to poll.
explain_choice: One request with one reply is exactly what plain HTTP is for; a persistent socket adds cost and nothing else.
WebSocket frames bypass HTTP caching entirely; cacheable data suits plain GET requests.
For rare updates, an idle connection per client for hours costs more than an occasional poll.

questions.prompt: Your page's `fetch()` to another origin fails with a CORS error. Where is that rule enforced?
choices: On the server, which refuses to answer requests from other origins
In the browser, based on headers in the server's response
In a firewall or proxy between the page and the API
In every HTTP client, including curl and requests
questions.explain: The same-origin policy is a browser rule that protects the user's cookies and sessions from other sites' scripts. For a simple request the browser sends it, reads the response's Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and hides the body from the page if the origin is not allowed. So the server may well have done the work. curl and requests have no such policy, which is why the call works from a terminal.
explain_choice: The server only states a policy in its headers; the request often reaches it and is processed, and it is the browser that withholds the response.
No network device takes part; the check happens inside the browser after the response arrives.
Command-line clients ignore CORS entirely, which is why the same request succeeds from a terminal.

questions.prompt: Your dev server listens on 127.0.0.1:8000. A phone on the same Wi-Fi can't reach it at your laptop's IP. Why?
choices: Phones can only reach servers over HTTPS on port 443
Port 8000 is reserved for local use and can't be reached remotely
127.0.0.1 is loopback, which only accepts connections from this machine
127.0.0.1 is the router's address, so the phone's requests are sent there
questions.explain: A listening socket is bound to one address. The loopback interface never carries traffic from other machines, so a server bound to 127.0.0.1 is unreachable from the network whatever the firewall says. Bind to 0.0.0.0, meaning all interfaces, or to the laptop's LAN address, and then check the firewall.
explain_choice: Phones can make plain HTTP requests to any port; the refusal comes from the bind address.
Ports above 1023 are unprivileged and have no local-only rule; what makes it local is the address the socket is bound to.
127.0.0.1 is every machine's own loopback address; the router has an ordinary LAN address, often 192.168.x.1.

questions.prompt: You change a DNS A record, but an hour later some users still reach the old server. Why?
choices: The old server still holds the certificate, so traffic sticks to it
DNS changes go out to all resolvers in one nightly batch
Every root server must copy your change, which takes up to 72 hours
Resolvers and clients cache the old record until its TTL runs out
questions.explain: A resolver that looked up your name keeps the answer for the record's TTL, and operating systems, browsers and language runtimes may cache it too; some keep it longer than the TTL. Nothing is pushed out: each cache expires on its own clock. Lowering the TTL a day before a planned move keeps the switch short.
explain_choice: Certificates play no part in choosing an IP address; the client connects to whatever address its cached DNS answer gives.
There is no push or batch; each cache holds the answer until its TTL expires, then asks again.
Root servers only point to the servers for each top-level domain; your record lives on your own authoritative servers and is never copied to the roots.

questions.prompt: `requests.get(url, timeout=10)` hits a server that sends one byte every five seconds, forever. What happens?
choices: It never times out, since 10 s bounds each wait for data
It returns the partial body after 10 seconds
It raises at once, since the reads are too slow
It raises Timeout once 10 seconds of total elapsed time have passed
questions.explain: In requests the timeout applies to the connect and then to each wait for the next bytes on the socket, not to the whole call. A trickle that never pauses for 10 seconds resets the clock on every byte, so the call runs indefinitely. A real budget needs an overall deadline, for example streaming the body and checking elapsed time, or an HTTP client with a total timeout.
explain_choice: requests has no 'return what you have' behaviour; a timeout raises an exception.
Slowness alone does not trigger it; only a gap longer than the timeout between bytes does.
requests has no total-time timeout; the number bounds each read, so a slow but steady server never trips it.

questions.prompt: A session cookie is set with the HttpOnly flag. What does that protect against?
choices: Page JavaScript reading it, so an XSS bug can't simply steal it
The user editing its value in their own browser
Being attached to requests that other sites trigger
Being sent over plain HTTP, where anyone on the network could read it
questions.explain: HttpOnly hides the cookie from `document.cookie` and other script APIs while the browser still sends it with requests. That removes the easiest payoff of an XSS bug, copying the session token to an attacker. Each of the other threats has its own flag or defence: Secure for plain HTTP, SameSite for cross-site requests, and a server-side signature for tampering.
explain_choice: Users can always edit their own cookies; only a server-side signature or lookup detects tampering.
That is the SameSite attribute, the main browser-side defence against CSRF.
That is the Secure flag, which keeps the cookie off unencrypted connections.

questions.prompt: `authors LEFT JOIN books ON books.author_id = authors.id` returns:
choices: Every author, once per matching book, with NULLs where there is none
Every author exactly once, with at most one matching book beside each
Only the authors who have at least one matching book
Every author and every book, NULL-filled on either side
questions.explain: A left join starts from the inner join, where each author is repeated once per matching book, then adds back every author with no match, padding the book columns with NULL. So an author with three books appears three times. A WHERE clause on a books column, such as `WHERE books.year > 2000`, discards those NULL rows and quietly turns it back into an inner join.
explain_choice: Joins never collapse matches: an author with three books appears on three rows.
That is an inner join; a left join keeps the unmatched left rows too.
Keeping unmatched rows from both sides is a FULL OUTER JOIN.

questions.prompt: An index speeds up reads. What does it cost?
choices: Nothing once built, since the planner simply skips it when it doesn't help
Slower writes and more storage, since each write updates it too
Slower reads on other columns, which must scan around it
Just disk space; inserts and updates run at the same speed
questions.explain: An index is a second sorted structure that must stay consistent with the table, so every INSERT, every DELETE and any UPDATE of an indexed column also modifies each index, and every index takes space on disk and in cache. Ten unused indexes on a busy table can make writes several times slower for no gain.
explain_choice: The planner can ignore an index on reads, but writes must still maintain it; that cost never goes away.
An index on one column does not change how other columns are read; its cost falls on writes and space.
Every insert and delete touches every index on the table, so writes slow down as indexes accumulate.

questions.prompt: Does a B-tree index on `(a, b)` help `WHERE b = 5` when the query doesn't mention `a`?
choices: No, and it can't serve `WHERE a = 5` on its own either
Yes, a composite index serves a lookup on any one of its columns equally
Usually not: entries are ordered by a first, and by b only within each a
Yes, but only if b has fewer distinct values than a
questions.explain: A composite index is ordered like a phone book by surname, then first name: all b = 5 entries are scattered across every value of a, so there is no contiguous range to jump to. Filtering on a alone, or on a and b, uses the ordering directly. Some engines can use a skip scan, including PostgreSQL 18, but that only pays off when a has few distinct values.
explain_choice: A leading prefix is exactly what a composite index serves well; `WHERE a = 5` uses it directly.
The sort order is by a first, so only a leading prefix of the columns can be searched as a range.
It is the leading column's distinct count that matters, and only for engines with skip scan; with few values of a they can visit each one.

questions.prompt: What does a transaction's atomicity guarantee?
choices: It runs as if no other transaction ran at the same time
Other sessions can't see its changes until it commits
Its committed changes survive a crash or power loss
All of its changes take effect, or none of them do
questions.explain: Atomicity is the A in ACID: if any statement fails, or the connection drops before COMMIT, the database rolls back everything the transaction did, so a transfer never debits one account without crediting the other. Visibility to other sessions is isolation, and surviving a crash is durability; they are separate guarantees with separate settings.
explain_choice: Behaving as if run alone is serializability, the strictest isolation level, which most databases do not use by default.
Hiding uncommitted changes from others is isolation, the I in ACID.
Surviving a crash after commit is durability, the D in ACID, provided by the write-ahead log.

questions.prompt: Transaction A holds a lock B needs, while B holds a lock A needs. What happens in PostgreSQL?
choices: The database merges both into one transaction and commits it
It detects the deadlock and aborts one of them with an error
Both wait until the statement timeout, if one has been set
The second writer wins, and the first writer's update is lost
questions.explain: Neither can proceed, so the database checks for a cycle in its lock waits (after deadlock_timeout, one second by default) and aborts one transaction with a deadlock error, releasing its locks so the other finishes. Your code must catch that error and retry the whole transaction. Taking locks in a consistent order, such as by ascending id, prevents it.
explain_choice: Transactions are never merged; one is chosen as the victim and rolled back.
PostgreSQL does not rely on a timeout; its deadlock detector breaks the cycle within about a second.
A lost update is a different problem that happens without any lock wait; here both are blocked.

questions.prompt: What is the N+1 query problem?
choices: Forgetting a WHERE clause, so a query reads N+1 rows too many
Adding one index too many, so every write updates N+1 indexes
Fetching a list, then running one more query per item for related data
A join that duplicates each row once per extra matching child
questions.explain: An ORM that loads relations lazily runs one query for the list and then, when your loop touches `book.author`, one query per book: 1 + N round trips, each with its own network and parse cost. It is invisible in a unit test with three rows and slow in production. Eager loading (a join, or one IN query per relation) makes it a constant number of queries.
explain_choice: A missing WHERE reads too much data in one query; N+1 is many small queries.
It is about the number of queries sent, not the number of indexes.
Row duplication from a join is a separate effect; N+1 is what happens when you avoid the join.

questions.prompt: What does `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` give you that plain `EXPLAIN` does not?
choices: It runs the query and reports real row counts and timings per step
It checks the syntax and refreshes the table's statistics
It shows the plan the planner would choose, without running the query
It recommends the indexes that would make the query faster
questions.explain: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan with the planner's estimates. ANALYZE also executes it and shows the actual rows and time at each node, so you can spot where estimates diverge from reality, often the real cause of a bad plan. Because it executes the query, wrap an UPDATE or DELETE in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK.
explain_choice: Refreshing statistics is the separate ANALYZE command; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query.
That is what plain EXPLAIN does; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query.
PostgreSQL recommends nothing; you read the plan and decide on an index yourself.

questions.prompt: What does a foreign key constraint mainly give you?
choices: Faster joins, because the referencing column gets indexed automatically
A relationship the ORM can follow without extra configuration
Deleting a parent row deletes its child rows automatically
The database refuses rows that point at a parent that doesn't exist
questions.explain: The constraint makes the database check every insert and update on the child, and every delete of a parent, so orphaned rows cannot exist however many code paths write to the tables. It does not index the referencing column in PostgreSQL, so add one yourself if you join or delete by it. Cascading deletes happen only with ON DELETE CASCADE.
explain_choice: PostgreSQL indexes the referenced key but not the referencing column; MySQL's InnoDB creates one, which is where the belief comes from.
ORMs declare relationships in their own models; the constraint is about the database enforcing integrity.
The default action is to reject the delete; cascading needs ON DELETE CASCADE.

questions.prompt: Why does a web app need a database connection pool?
choices: A pool lets one connection run several queries in parallel
Pooled connections are encrypted, whereas one-off connections are not
New connections are slow to open, and servers cap how many can exist
A pool caches query results, so repeated reads skip the database
questions.explain: Each new PostgreSQL connection costs a TCP handshake, often TLS, authentication and a new server process. Servers cap the total (max_connections, 100 by default). A pool keeps a few connections open and lends them out per request, so under load you queue for a connection instead of exhausting the server's limit.
explain_choice: A connection runs one query at a time; a pool gives concurrency by holding several connections.
Encryption is set per connection (TLS) and is unrelated to pooling.
Pools reuse connections, not results; every query still runs on the server.

questions.prompt: To list customers with more than five orders, why does `WHERE COUNT(*) > 5` fail?
choices: WHERE can't reference columns that aren't in the SELECT list
It works, but linters reject it because HAVING is the faster form
COUNT(*) includes NULLs, so a WHERE needs COUNT(id)
WHERE filters rows before grouping, so no count exists yet
questions.explain: A query is evaluated FROM, then WHERE on individual rows, then GROUP BY, then HAVING on each group, then SELECT. An aggregate only has a value once rows are grouped, so the condition belongs in HAVING: `GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`. Row filters that do not need an aggregate stay in WHERE, where they shrink the input before grouping.
explain_choice: WHERE can use any column of the FROM tables; the problem is the aggregate, not the column list.
It is not a style warning; SQL rejects aggregates in WHERE with an error.
The NULL handling of COUNT is unrelated; any aggregate in WHERE is an error because grouping has not happened yet.

questions.prompt: `email` is indexed, yet `WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com'` does a full table scan. Why?
choices: B-tree indexes suit numeric columns, not text columns like email
The index is on email, not lower(email), so it can't be searched
Equality on strings needs a hash index rather than a B-tree
Wrapping a column in any function in WHERE disables every index on the table
questions.explain: The index stores email values sorted as written, and the planner cannot search it for the result of lower() without computing lower() for every row. Either create an expression index, `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))`, or store the email in a normalised form and compare it directly. Other indexes on the table are unaffected.
explain_choice: B-trees order text perfectly well; the problem is that the query asks about a different expression.
B-trees handle equality as well as ranges; a hash index would have the same problem with lower().
Only the wrapped column loses its index; an expression index on the same function is used normally.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL at the default READ COMMITTED level, two transactions both run `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1`. What happens?
choices: The second waits for the lock, then subtracts from the updated balance
Both read the old balance, so one of the two deductions is silently lost
They deadlock, and the database aborts one of them
The second fails with a serialization error and must be retried
questions.explain: The first UPDATE takes a row lock. The second blocks on it, and once the first commits it re-reads the latest version of the row and subtracts from that, so both deductions apply. Lost updates happen when the application reads the balance, computes in Python and writes back an absolute value; keeping the arithmetic in SQL, or using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, avoids them.
explain_choice: That is the read-modify-write pattern done in application code; a single UPDATE re-checks the row after waiting for the lock.
A deadlock needs two locks taken in opposite orders; here both want the same single row lock, so one simply waits.
Serialization failures come from REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE; READ COMMITTED waits and re-reads instead.

questions.prompt: Why can a CTE (`WITH ...`) be slow in PostgreSQL 11 but fast in 12 and later?
choices: From 12, indexes are no longer allowed inside a CTE
From 12, CTE results are cached across queries and sessions
Before 12 CTEs were always materialised, so outer filters couldn't reach in
Before 12 a CTE was re-run once for every row of the query that referenced it
questions.explain: Up to version 11 a CTE was an optimisation fence: it was computed in full into a temporary result, so a later `WHERE id = 5` could not be pushed into it to use an index. Since 12, a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined like a subquery. `AS MATERIALIZED` and `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` let you choose explicitly.
explain_choice: Indexes are used inside CTEs in every version; the change was about inlining.
PostgreSQL has no cross-query result cache; each query computes its CTEs afresh.
That describes a correlated subquery; a CTE was computed once per query, which was the problem.

questions.prompt: Why does `SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at = NULL` return no rows, even for users never deleted?
choices: It matches only rows inserted after the column was added
Comparing anything with = NULL gives unknown, never true; use IS NULL
NULL can't be compared at all, so the query errors out and returns nothing
It matches only rows where the column holds the text 'NULL'
questions.explain: SQL uses three-valued logic: NULL means 'unknown', so `x = NULL` evaluates to unknown for every x, including NULL itself, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` are the tests for missing values. The same logic makes `NOT IN (subquery)` return nothing if the subquery yields a NULL.
explain_choice: Rows added before the column exists hold NULL like any other; the comparison fails for them all equally.
The query runs without error; each comparison is simply unknown, so no row passes.
The literal NULL is not a string; comparing with the text 'NULL' would be `= 'NULL'`.

questions.prompt: How do authentication and authorisation differ?
choices: They are the same check, both done by the login middleware
Authentication proves identity to users; authorisation proves it to APIs
Authentication establishes who you are; authorisation, what you may do
Authorisation checks the password; authentication then checks the role
questions.explain: Authentication answers 'who is this?' once per request, from a password, token or certificate. Authorisation then answers 'may this identity do this to this object?', a separate decision that depends on the resource. The two fail independently: a flawless login does nothing to stop user 7 fetching `/invoices/8`, and broken object-level authorisation is the most common API vulnerability.
explain_choice: Login middleware establishes identity only; whether that identity may touch a given object is checked separately.
Both apply to any caller, human or machine; the split is identity versus permission, not audience.
That reverses them: checking a password is authentication, and roles and permissions are authorisation.

questions.prompt: Where must access control be enforced?
choices: In the frontend, by hiding what the user may not use
Always on the server, for each request and each object touched
Once at login, then trusted for the rest of the user's session
At the API gateway only, so handlers can stay simple
questions.explain: Anyone can send HTTP requests with curl, skipping your UI entirely, and change an ID in the URL. So the server must check, on each request, that this user may perform this action on this specific object. A gateway can reject unauthenticated traffic, but it does not know who owns invoice 8; only the code that loads the invoice does.
explain_choice: Hiding buttons is good UX but no protection: the request can be crafted directly without the page.
Permissions change and objects differ per request; a login proves identity, not the right to each resource.
A gateway can check the token but not object-level ownership, which needs the application's data.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off of a stateless JWT compared with a server-side session?
choices: It can't easily be revoked before expiry, as the server keeps no record
It works on a single server, where sessions scale out
It has to be looked up in the database on every request
It is encrypted, so the client can't read the claims inside it
questions.explain: The server trusts a JWT because its signature checks out, so nothing needs to be looked up, and that is also why it cannot be cancelled: a stolen token stays valid until `exp`. Short-lived access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens, or a denylist, recover some control. Signed JWTs are only base64url-encoded, so anyone holding one can read its claims.
explain_choice: It is sessions that need shared storage to work across servers; any server with the key can verify a JWT.
Avoiding a per-request lookup is the whole point of a self-contained token; the cost is revocation.
A standard signed JWT (JWS) is readable by anyone who base64-decodes it; never put secrets in its claims.

questions.prompt: How should passwords be stored?
choices: As SHA-512, since a longer hash takes longer to brute-force
As SHA-256 with a per-user salt, since the salt defeats rainbow tables
Encrypted with AES, the key kept in an environment variable
With a slow, salted password hash such as argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt
questions.explain: An attacker who steals the table tries guesses offline, so what matters is the cost per guess. A salt only stops precomputed tables and identical passwords sharing a hash; SHA-256 is designed to be fast, billions per second on a GPU. Password hashes are tuned to be slow, and argon2id and scrypt also make each guess need lots of memory, which defeats GPUs.
explain_choice: Digest length has little effect on guessing cost; SHA-512 is still built to be fast.
Salting blocks rainbow tables, but a fast hash still lets an attacker test billions of guesses per second.
Encryption is reversible: whoever gets the key, often from the same server, gets every password.

questions.prompt: Why does `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` pagination break down on large tables?
choices: OFFSET needs an index on the sort column, so it fails on unindexed tables
The database reads and discards every skipped row, and rows shift as data changes
Clients can't jump straight to a page number, as they can with cursor pagination
SQL doesn't guarantee OFFSET works together with an ORDER BY clause
questions.explain: OFFSET is not a seek: to skip 100,000 rows the database produces them in order and throws them away, so page 5,000 costs far more than page 1. And if a row is inserted or deleted before the current page between requests, items move across page boundaries and get repeated or skipped. Cursor (keyset) pagination, `WHERE (created, id) > (:last_created, :last_id)`, seeks straight to the position through an index.
explain_choice: OFFSET works without an index; it is just slow either way at depth, because the skipped rows are still produced.
That reverses them: jumping to page N is offset's strength and cursor pagination's limitation.
OFFSET with ORDER BY is standard and deterministic when the sort key is unique; the problems are cost and drift.

questions.prompt: What do Pydantic models in a FastAPI route mainly give you?
choices: Parsed, validated request and response data, plus the OpenAPI schema
Authentication, since the model checks the fields of the caller's token
Faster routing, since the models are compiled into native code
Database access, since each model maps to a table like an ORM
questions.explain: FastAPI reads the type hints on your route, parses the body and parameters with Pydantic, rejects bad input with a 422 listing each field error, and filters output through the response model. The same models produce the OpenAPI schema and the /docs page. So the handler's body can trust the shape of its data.
explain_choice: Authentication is handled by security dependencies; a model can describe a token's shape but checks no credentials.
pydantic-core is written in Rust, but that speeds up validation; route matching is Starlette's job and unrelated.
Pydantic models are not tied to tables; SQLModel combines the two, but Pydantic alone does no persistence.

questions.prompt: What does putting a request ID on every log line let you do?
choices: Sort log lines back into the order that requests arrived
Rate-limit each client by counting its request IDs
Drop duplicate retries, since a retried request keeps its original ID
Pull out every line for one request from many interleaved ones
questions.explain: Under concurrency, lines from dozens of requests interleave in one stream, so 'the error after the query' may belong to a different user. Middleware generates or accepts an ID, stores it in a contextvar, and the log formatter adds it to every line, including lines from downstream services if you forward the header. Filtering on one ID reconstructs one request's path.
explain_choice: Timestamps order lines; the ID groups them by request, which a timestamp cannot.
Rate limiting counts by client identity, such as a key or IP; a request ID is unique per request.
Each attempt usually gets a new request ID; recognising a duplicate is the job of an idempotency key.

questions.prompt: Is returning a stack trace in an API error response acceptable in production?
choices: Yes, because users can include it in the bug reports they send you
Yes, if the API is only called by your own frontend and never by users
Never: it leaks paths, versions and code that help an attacker map the system
Yes, once the service is behind HTTPS, as nobody else can read it
questions.explain: A trace shows file paths, library versions, SQL fragments and the shape of your code, a free reconnaissance report for the person causing errors on purpose. Log it server-side with a correlation ID and return a generic message containing that ID; support can then find the full trace without exposing it.
explain_choice: An error ID in the response gives support the same trace from the logs without handing it to every caller.
Anyone can call the API directly, bypassing your frontend, and see the same response.
HTTPS hides it from eavesdroppers, but the attacker is the client receiving the response.

questions.prompt: Why is running background work inside the web process (such as FastAPI's BackgroundTasks) risky for important jobs?
choices: The response is held back until every background task has finished
Queued work lives in memory and is lost when the process stops or crashes
A second worker process is needed for them to run at all
Background tasks can no longer write to the logs once the request has ended
questions.explain: In-process tasks run after the response is sent, in the same process, with no record anywhere else. A deploy, an autoscaler removing the instance or an out-of-memory kill takes pending work with it, and nothing retries it. Work that must happen, such as sending a receipt, belongs in a durable queue whose worker acknowledges a job only after it completes.
explain_choice: FastAPI sends the response first and then runs the tasks; the problem is durability, not latency.
They run in the same process with no extra worker, which is exactly why a restart loses them.
Logging works as normal in background tasks; only the request's own scope has ended.

questions.prompt: A FastAPI route declares `db = Depends(get_db)`. How should a test make it use a test database?
choices: Put a test-session function in `app.dependency_overrides[get_db]`
Set an environment variable that `get_db` reads when first imported
Pass the test session as a query parameter named `db` in the request
Monkeypatch `get_db` in its own module after the app has been imported
questions.explain: Depends stores a reference to the get_db function object when the route is defined, and FastAPI looks up overrides by that same object. Rebinding the module attribute later changes nothing the route holds. dependency_overrides swaps it where FastAPI resolves dependencies; clear it after each test.
explain_choice: A value read at import time is fixed before the test can set it; overrides act at request time instead.
Dependencies are not request parameters; a client cannot supply them.
The route captured the original function object when it was defined, so rebinding the name in the module has no effect.

questions.prompt: `alembic revision --autogenerate` has written a migration. What next?
choices: Commit it unread, since CI applies every migration in order anyway
Delete it and call `create_all()`, which does the same thing more simply
Apply it straight away, since it was generated from the models and must be right
Read and edit it; it misses some changes and turns renames into drop-and-add
questions.explain: Autogenerate diffs your models against the live schema. It cannot tell a renamed column from a dropped column plus a new one, which would destroy the data, and it misses some changes such as certain constraint and server-default edits. It also writes no data migrations. Treat its output as a draft to review.
explain_choice: CI running it in order does not make a wrong migration right; the data loss just happens in every environment.
create_all only creates missing tables; it never alters existing ones, and it keeps no version history.
It compares structure, not intent: a renamed column appears as a drop and an add, and running that loses the column's data.

questions.prompt: Your API tests pass one at a time but fail when the whole suite runs. The usual cause is:
choices: Fixtures get rebuilt for every single test, which makes later tests time out
pytest runs the tests in parallel by default, and they collide
The tests share database state, so one test's rows leak into the next
The test client caches responses between the tests that use it
questions.explain: A test that inserts a user and never cleans up changes what the next test's queries return, so results depend on order. The standard fix is to run each test inside a transaction that is rolled back at teardown, or use a fresh database per test, so every test starts from the same state.
explain_choice: Function-scoped fixtures being rebuilt is what gives isolation; it makes tests slower, not wrong.
pytest runs tests serially unless you add a plugin such as pytest-xdist.
The test client does not cache responses; each call goes through the app.

questions.prompt: How should an upload endpoint decide whether a file is an acceptable image?
choices: Check the filename's extension against an allow-list of image types
Trust the Content-Type header that the browser sent along with the file
Rely on the form's `accept=` attribute to stop other file types
Cap the size while reading, then check the bytes themselves
questions.explain: Everything the client sends about the file, including name, extension and Content-Type, is chosen by the client and can say anything. The server should stop reading past a size limit, so a 10 GB upload cannot fill the disk, then check the bytes: magic numbers at minimum, or actually decoding the image. Store it under a generated name, never the one supplied.
explain_choice: Renaming `payload.exe` to `cat.png` takes a second; the extension says nothing about the content.
The Content-Type is set by the client and can be any string an attacker likes.
`accept=` only filters the browser's file picker; a direct request ignores it.

quizzes.name: Automation & web
quizzes.desc: Work that runs while you sleep.

questions.prompt: A setup job creates folders, writes a config file and registers a webhook. Which step design keeps a second run harmless?
choices: Each step checks the current state and acts only to reach the target
Each step writes a 'done' marker before it starts, then does its work
The scheduler guarantees it fires once, so reruns can't happen
The whole job is wrapped in try/except so reruns can't fail
questions.explain: A convergent step describes an end state rather than an action: `mkdir(exist_ok=True)`, write the config only if it differs, look up the webhook before creating it. Run it once or five times and the system ends up the same, which covers manual reruns, crashes part way through and a scheduler firing twice. Marking a step done before doing it gives the opposite: a crash between the two leaves the work skipped forever.
explain_choice: If the job crashes after writing the marker and before the work, reruns skip that step for good; a marker belongs after the work.
Schedulers do fire twice (retries, failovers, clock changes), and people rerun jobs by hand; the job itself must tolerate it.
Swallowing exceptions hides failures; the second run still creates a duplicate webhook, it just does so silently.

questions.prompt: Your scraper breaks every week or two. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The site blocks the scraper's User-Agent string each week
Its selectors rely on generated class names or deep layout paths
The parsing library changes its API in each minor release
The site rate-limits it, which returns an empty page instead of data
questions.explain: Front-end build tools generate class names such as `.css-1x7fq2` that change on every deploy, and paths like `div > div:nth-child(3) > span` break whenever a wrapper is added. Anchor on things the site keeps stable for its own reasons, such as ids, `data-*` attributes, ARIA labels or visible text, and make the scraper fail loudly when an expected field is missing rather than saving blanks.
explain_choice: A blocked User-Agent gives 403s or captchas; a changed page with a 200 status points at the markup.
Parsers such as BeautifulSoup and lxml keep stable APIs; weekly breakage tracks the site's deploys, not library releases.
Rate limiting shows up as 429 responses or blocks, usually immediately, not as a weekly selector failure.

questions.prompt: An API answers 429 Too Many Requests. What should your client do?
choices: Switch to another IP address so the limit no longer applies
Retry at once, since 429 just means the server is busy for now
Wait before retrying, using the Retry-After value when it is sent
Drop the task as a permanent failure and move on to the next
questions.explain: 429 is the server telling you to slow down. Retry-After, when present, says how many seconds (or until what date) to wait; otherwise back off exponentially with jitter. Then lower your sending rate, because a client that keeps hitting the limit tends to get blocked for longer. The task itself is still valid and should be retried, not dropped.
explain_choice: Rotating IPs to dodge a limit is evasion that breaks most terms of service and gets keys revoked.
Retrying at once is precisely what the limit is there to stop, and repeated violations often escalate to longer blocks.
The request was fine; it needs to be sent later, not discarded.

questions.prompt: When do you need Playwright rather than a plain HTTP client like requests?
choices: When the site sets cookies, which requests can't keep between calls
When the site is slow, since a browser waits more patiently for it
When the page is very large, since a browser streams it more efficiently
When the content is built by JavaScript after the page's HTML loads
questions.explain: An HTTP client receives the initial HTML and runs no scripts, so anything the page fetches and renders with JavaScript is missing. A real browser executes those scripts. Before reaching for one, check the network tab: the page often loads its data from a JSON endpoint you can call directly, which is faster and far more stable.
explain_choice: `requests.Session()` stores and resends cookies automatically; cookies alone do not need a browser.
Timeouts are configurable in any client; a browser is slower and heavier, not more patient.
A full browser downloads and renders far more than the HTML; for a large static page an HTTP client is cheaper.

questions.prompt: What should a webhook receiver do when a delivery arrives?
choices: Skip signature checks, since the endpoint URL is kept secret
Call the sender's API to confirm the event before replying
Do all the work first, then respond, so the sender knows it worked
Verify the signature, queue the work, and return 2xx quickly
questions.explain: Senders wait only a few seconds and then treat the delivery as failed and send it again, so slow inline processing causes duplicates. Verifying the HMAC signature over the raw body proves the sender and the content; then persist the event, reply 2xx and process from the queue, deduplicating on the event ID because retries still happen.
explain_choice: URLs leak through logs, proxies and screenshots; the signature is what proves who sent it.
An extra API call before replying adds latency and a new failure point; the signature already proves authenticity.
Long processing risks the sender's timeout, which triggers a redelivery and duplicate work.

questions.prompt: What should you check before scraping a site?
choices: Its terms of service, robots.txt, and whether an official API exists
Nothing, if the data is publicly visible without logging in
Only robots.txt, since that file is what grants legal permission to scrape
That you send a realistic browser User-Agent so you blend in
questions.explain: An official API is usually faster, more stable and explicitly allowed. The terms of service set what the owner permits, and robots.txt says which paths automated clients should avoid; neither alone is the whole picture, and both affect whether you keep access. Rate-limit yourself and identify your client honestly.
explain_choice: Being publicly viewable does not grant permission for automated copying; terms and rate limits still apply.
robots.txt is a convention for crawlers, not a licence; the terms of service and applicable law still apply.
Disguising the client is the opposite of respectful crawling and often breaches the terms.

questions.prompt: A job crashes after processing 6,000 of 10,000 items. What does good design let you do?
choices: Rerun with smaller batches, so the next crash loses less work
Resume from saved progress, skipping items already completed
Start over, since partial results from a crash can't be trusted
Retry the whole job in a loop until one full run completes
questions.explain: If each item's completion is recorded durably, in the same transaction as its result or right after an idempotent write, the rerun reads that record and continues from item 6,001. Starting over repeats work and side effects such as emails, and whole-job retries do the same on every failure. Checkpointing is what turns a crash into a short delay.
explain_choice: Smaller batches reduce what one crash loses, but without saved progress you still restart from the beginning.
Results committed per item are trustworthy; redoing them repeats side effects such as emails or charges.
Each retry redoes all the completed items, and a persistent failure loops forever.

questions.prompt: Where should an automation script's API keys and passwords live?
choices: In the source, base64-encoded so a quick glance can't read them
In a `.env` file committed so teammates can run the script
In environment variables or a secret manager, kept out of Git
In the script, since the repository is private to you
questions.explain: Anything committed stays in the repository's history, which is cloned, forked, backed up and sometimes made public. Deleting the line later does not remove it. Load secrets at run time from the environment or a secret manager, keep `.env` in .gitignore, and rotate any key that was ever committed.
explain_choice: base64 is an encoding, not encryption; anyone can decode it in one command.
A committed .env is a committed secret; share an example file with placeholders instead.
Private repositories get shared, forked, made public and cloned onto laptops; the secret is in every copy of the history.

questions.prompt: A Playwright script sometimes fails to click a button that appears after a request. What is the robust fix?
choices: Rerun the whole script automatically until one attempt succeeds
Run the browser headed, since headless mode skips drawing some buttons
Add `time.sleep(5)` before the click to give the page time
Use locator actions that auto-wait, or wait for a specific condition
questions.explain: Timing varies from run to run, so a fixed sleep is either too short on a slow day or wasted time on a fast one. Playwright's locator actions wait until the element is attached, visible, stable and enabled before acting, and `expect(...)` or `wait_for_response` waits for a named condition. Waiting on the condition you actually need removes the race rather than guessing its length.
explain_choice: Retrying hides a race rather than fixing it, and repeats side effects of the earlier steps.
Headless browsers render the same DOM; differences come from viewport size or timing, not skipped elements.
A sleep guesses a duration; it still fails on a slow run and slows every fast one.

questions.prompt: Your job's OAuth access token expires after an hour, but the job runs for six. What should it do?
choices: Keep using the old token, since expiry is just a suggestion
Store the user's password and log in again every hour
Use the refresh token to get a new access token when it expires
Request a token with no expiry, which most servers grant if you ask for one
questions.explain: OAuth separates a short-lived access token, sent with every call, from a longer-lived refresh token, sent only to the token endpoint. When the access token expires, or a call returns 401, exchange the refresh token for a new pair and retry once. Store the refresh token as a secret, and save the new one if the server rotates it.
explain_choice: The resource server checks `exp` and rejects expired tokens with 401.
Holding the password defeats the point of OAuth, and many providers do not allow a password grant at all.
Lifetimes are the provider's policy; a client cannot ask for a token that never expires.

questions.prompt: A job scheduled every five minutes sometimes takes seven. What stops two copies running at once?
choices: Check `ps` at start for another process with the script's name
Take an exclusive lock at start, such as flock, and exit if it is held
Nothing is needed: cron waits for one run to finish before starting the next
Move the schedule to every ten minutes so the runs can't overlap
questions.explain: cron starts each run on the clock whether or not the last one has finished. An atomic lock taken at start, such as `flock -n /tmp/job.lock` or a database advisory lock, lets exactly one run proceed, and the operating system releases it if the holder dies. A check followed by a separate start leaves a window in which both runs pass the check.
explain_choice: Two runs can both check `ps` before either appears in it; the check and the claim must be one atomic step.
cron has no idea a previous run is still going; it starts a new one every time the schedule matches.
A longer interval only moves the problem: the day the job takes eleven minutes, runs overlap again.

questions.prompt: An API response carries `Link: <https://api.example.com/items?cursor=abc>; rel="next"`. How should you page through the results?
choices: Follow the rel="next" URL each time until a response has none
Pass page=all to fetch every result in a single request
Read the total count and build every page URL before you start
Increment a page number yourself until a page comes back empty
questions.explain: The server hands you the exact URL of the next page, often with an opaque cursor, so the client does not need to know how pagination works. Stop when no rel="next" is present. Building URLs yourself breaks when the API uses cursors, and it skips or repeats items when data changes mid-walk. requests exposes the parsed header as `response.links`.
explain_choice: APIs cap page size to protect themselves; there is no standard page=all.
Counts go stale while you page, and a cursor-based API cannot be addressed by page number at all.
The URL carries a cursor, not a page number; guessing numbers breaks as soon as the API changes scheme.

quizzes.name: Async & performance
quizzes.desc: Choosing a concurrency model and proving it.

questions.prompt: On the default (GIL-enabled) CPython build, what does the GIL stop?
choices: Threads from overlapping at all, so threading gives no speed-up on I/O waits
Two threads in one process running Python bytecode at the same instant
Data races in your code, so a shared counter needs no lock around it
Several processes from running Python code on separate cores at once
questions.explain: Only the thread holding the GIL may execute bytecode, but blocking I/O calls and many C extensions release it while they wait, so I/O-bound threads still overlap. It protects the interpreter's own state, not your invariants: a thread switch can still land between the steps of your own compound operation. Since 3.14 the free-threaded build (python3.14t, PEP 703, officially supported under PEP 779) has no GIL at all and runs bytecode in parallel, but the GIL build remains the default.
explain_choice: The GIL is released during blocking I/O, so threads waiting on sockets or files do overlap, which is why threads help I/O-bound work.
The GIL keeps CPython's internals consistent, not your data: `counter += 1` is several bytecodes and a switch can fall between them.
Each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, so processes run truly in parallel; that is why multiprocessing exists.

questions.prompt: On the default CPython build, what makes pure-Python CPU-bound work use several cores?
choices: A thread pool sized to match the core count, so that no core is left sitting idle
More threads, because the operating system gives each thread its own core
Separate processes, or native code that releases the GIL while it computes
asyncio tasks, because the event loop spreads coroutines over the cores
questions.explain: Each process has its own interpreter and GIL, so the cores really run in parallel; the price is pickling arguments and results across the process boundary. Python 3.14 adds two more routes: per-interpreter GIL (PEP 684, in the C API since 3.12) exposed as `concurrent.interpreters` and `InterpreterPoolExecutor` (PEP 734), and the optional free-threaded build (PEP 703/779), where plain threads do run bytecode in parallel.
explain_choice: Pool size does not matter while every worker queues for the same GIL; a ThreadPoolExecutor only helps work that releases it.
The OS will schedule threads on different cores, but on the GIL build only one of them can execute bytecode at a time, so the extra cores sit waiting.
An event loop runs on one thread; coroutines interleave at await points and never run at the same moment.

questions.prompt: A coroutine reaches `await` on something that is not ready yet. What happens?
choices: The awaited call is scheduled, and the coroutine carries on to the next line
The awaited call is handed to a worker thread from the default executor
Its thread blocks until the result arrives, just like an ordinary call
It suspends, and the event loop runs other ready tasks until it is able to resume
questions.explain: A coroutine is a resumable function: at a suspension point it returns control to the loop, which picks another ready task on the same thread and resumes this one when its future completes. That is how one thread serves thousands of sockets, and why any call that blocks without awaiting freezes the whole loop.
explain_choice: Execution does not continue past the await until the result is ready; to run something concurrently you create a task.
Nothing moves to a thread unless you ask for it with asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor; await alone stays on the loop's thread.
Blocking the thread is exactly what await avoids; the loop's thread moves on to other tasks while this one waits.

questions.prompt: What does calling `time.sleep(5)` inside an async function do?
choices: Stalls every task on that event loop for the full five seconds
Pauses just this coroutine, the same way asyncio.sleep(5) would
Nothing harmful; asyncio patches it into a non-blocking sleep
Raises RuntimeError, since blocking calls are banned in coroutines
questions.explain: time.sleep blocks the thread and never returns control to the loop, and every task on that loop shares the one thread, so none of them can run until it returns. Use `await asyncio.sleep(5)`, and push unavoidable blocking calls off the loop with `asyncio.to_thread`. Debug mode (PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1) logs callbacks that hog the loop, which is how you find these.
explain_choice: asyncio.sleep awaits a timer and yields to the loop; time.sleep holds the thread, so the whole loop stops with it.
asyncio does no monkey-patching of the standard library; that is gevent's approach, not asyncio's.
Python cannot tell a blocking call from any other call, so it runs silently; only debug mode warns you afterwards.

questions.prompt: You fire 10,000 requests at a third-party API with one unbounded `gather`. What is the likely result?
choices: Nothing much, since asyncio caps concurrent tasks by default
Local memory grows, but the API still sees one request at a time
429 responses, exhausted sockets, and possibly a blocked API key
It finishes about ten thousand times faster than a serial loop
questions.explain: gather starts every coroutine at once, so every request is in flight together. Servers protect themselves with rate limits and bans, and your side runs out of sockets and file descriptors. An `asyncio.Semaphore` or a fixed pool of workers reading a queue bounds how many are in flight, which is what makes a concurrent client polite and predictable.
explain_choice: asyncio puts no limit on tasks; any limit comes from the HTTP client's pool or from a semaphore you add yourself.
Every coroutine opens its own request as soon as gather schedules it, so the server sees them all at once.
Speed-up stops at whatever the server or the network allows; past that, extra concurrency only adds errors and retries.

questions.prompt: What does `asyncio.TaskGroup` give you that a bare `asyncio.gather` does not?
choices: When one child fails, the others are cancelled and all the errors raised together
The child tasks run truly in parallel, each on its own operating-system thread
Results come back in completion order rather than in submission order
Lower overhead, because it skips the scheduling step that gather performs
questions.explain: This is structured concurrency: the `async with` block does not exit until every child has finished, and on the first failure it cancels the siblings and raises all failures as an ExceptionGroup, handled with `except*`. Plain gather (without return_exceptions) raises the first exception but leaves the other tasks running unsupervised, where they can leak work or hide more errors.
explain_choice: A TaskGroup runs its tasks on the same event loop thread as gather does; neither uses threads.
Completion order is what asyncio.as_completed gives you; TaskGroup does not return results at all, you read them from the tasks.
The benefit is about lifetime and error handling, not speed; both schedule tasks the same way.

questions.prompt: A nightly report takes twenty minutes. What should you do before changing any code?
choices: Put a cache in front of the database calls, since I/O is usually where the cost is
Profile it, for example with cProfile, to see where the time actually goes
Rewrite the loop that looks slowest as a C extension, or with Cython
Spread the work over a thread pool, so all of the cores are kept busy
questions.explain: Guesses about where time goes are wrong often enough that measuring first is cheaper than optimising the wrong thing. cProfile's cumulative-time view shows which call dominates; then change one thing and measure again, so every speed-up is a number rather than a feeling.
explain_choice: Caching is a fix for one specific cause; if the time is spent in parsing or a quadratic loop, the cache does nothing.
Rewriting code that turns out not to be the bottleneck costs days and changes nothing; the profile tells you where C would pay off.
Threads on the GIL build do not speed up CPU-bound Python, and without a profile you do not know the work is CPU-bound anyway.

questions.prompt: Why do latency targets usually quote p95 or p99 rather than the mean?
choices: They measure how many requests per second the service is able to sustain
The mean is too expensive to calculate over millions of requests per minute
They are the mean with the outliers removed, so they are steadier over time
They show what the slowest 1 in 20 or 1 in 100 requests actually feel like
questions.explain: A few slow requests barely move the mean, so the mean can look healthy while real users wait. Tails also compound: a page that makes 20 backend calls hits at least one p95-slow call on about 64 per cent of loads (1 - 0.95^20), so the tail becomes the typical user experience.
explain_choice: That is throughput; latency percentiles describe how long individual requests take, not how many you can serve.
The mean is the cheapest statistic there is; percentiles are the costly ones, which is why tools use histograms to estimate them.
Percentiles keep the slow tail rather than trimming it; that tail is exactly what they are there to show.

questions.prompt: Two threads each run `counter += 1` a million times on a shared global, with no lock. What can happen?
choices: It stays exact, because the GIL turns each `+=` into one atomic bytecode step
It can go wrong on a machine with several cores, but not on a single core
It raises a RuntimeError when both threads write the variable at once
The total can come out short, because `+=` is a separate read, add and store
questions.explain: Correctness now depends on timing: if a thread switch falls between one thread's read and its store, the other thread's update is overwritten and lost. The loss may be rare on your machine and common in production, which is why shared mutable state needs a Lock (or a design with no sharing) rather than trust in the scheduler.
explain_choice: The GIL protects single bytecodes, and `+=` on a global compiles to several; the switch can fall between them.
Interleaving only needs a thread switch, which a single core does constantly; more cores just change how often it bites.
Python raises nothing for unsynchronised access; the corruption is silent, which is what makes races hard to find.

questions.prompt: You cancel an asyncio task that holds a database connection. What must its code do?
choices: Nothing: cancel() stops the task at once and frees everything it holds
Release it in a finally block, and re-raise CancelledError if the code catches it
Catch CancelledError and return normally, so the task ends without any error
Call loop.stop(), so no half-finished task is left running on the loop
questions.explain: cancel() does not kill anything: it raises CancelledError inside the coroutine at its next await, and only code in `finally` (or an `async with` exit) runs on the way out. Swallowing the error makes the task look as if it finished normally, which breaks TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout, both of which rely on the cancellation propagating.
explain_choice: Cancellation is cooperative: it arrives as an exception at an await point, and anything not released in cleanup code leaks.
Swallowing CancelledError hides the cancellation from whoever asked for it; timeouts and task groups then misbehave.
Stopping the loop abandons every task mid-flight, which leaks far more than the one connection you were worried about.

questions.prompt: Why copy requirements.txt and run pip install before `COPY . .` in a Dockerfile?
choices: It makes the final image smaller, because the install step skips the source
It changes nothing, since Docker caches every file by its name, whatever the order
Layers build in parallel, so putting the install first lets it start sooner
A code edit then rebuilds from the source COPY onwards, reusing the install layer
questions.explain: Each instruction's cache entry depends on its inputs and on every layer before it, so the first changed layer invalidates everything after it. Source changes on every commit while dependencies rarely do; putting the stable, expensive step first means an ordinary edit costs seconds instead of a full reinstall.
explain_choice: Both orders put the same files and packages in the final image; the ordering affects rebuild time, not size.
The cache is keyed per instruction and chained; a changed COPY invalidates every instruction below it.
Classic Dockerfile steps within one stage run in order; only separate stages can build concurrently.

questions.prompt: Your image runs as root. What does adding a non-root USER actually buy you?
choices: It limits what a code-execution bug in the container can reach
Volume mounts no longer need a chown on the host side
Faster start-up, because the kernel can skip its privilege checks
A smaller image, because root's home directory is left out of it
questions.explain: Without user-namespace remapping, root in the container is uid 0 on the host kernel, so a container escape or a mounted host path becomes a root compromise. A non-root user turns a remote-code-execution bug into a much smaller incident, which is why isolation is treated as one layer rather than the whole defence.
explain_choice: Ownership still has to match the uid the process runs as, so non-root often needs more chown work, not less.
Privilege checks cost the same for every user; the change is about damage, not speed.
The user an image runs as has no effect on its size; the layers are the same either way.

questions.prompt: What does a multi-stage Docker build let you do?
choices: Run all the build steps in parallel, so that the image finishes building sooner
Share one base layer between several services while they are running
Compile in a heavy build stage, then copy only the results into a slim one
Squash every layer into one, so the final image carries no history
questions.explain: Only what you `COPY --from=` the build stage reaches the final image, so compilers, headers and pip caches stay behind in a stage that is thrown away. The result is smaller and has less attack surface, because tools an attacker could use were never shipped.
explain_choice: Independent stages can build concurrently, but that is a side effect; the point is leaving the toolchain out of what ships.
Layer sharing between images happens through common base images, whether or not you use stages.
Squashing is a different feature; a multi-stage image still has layers, just none from the build stage.

questions.prompt: A Postgres container is removed and recreated from the same image. When does its data survive?
choices: When the container ran as root, so it could write to the host disk
When the data directory lives on a named volume or a bind mount
Every time, because the image keeps a copy of whatever was written
When you ran docker commit on the container before removing it
questions.explain: Writes go to a thin writable layer that belongs to the container: a restart keeps it, but removal deletes it. Volumes are managed outside the container's lifecycle, so a new container that mounts the same volume sees the old data. That is why state must live in a volume or an external store.
explain_choice: Running as root lets a process write inside the container, but the writable layer is still deleted with the container.
Images are read-only; each new container starts from the image's clean state, not from the last container's writes.
commit snapshots the container's layer into a new image, but it never captures volumes, which is where the Postgres image keeps its data.

questions.prompt: What is a container health check for?
choices: Exposing the service's port, so that other containers can reach it
Letting the platform tell serving from merely running, and then act on the result
Adding a start-up line to the logs, so you can see when it came up
Restarting the container automatically whenever its main process exits
questions.explain: A process can be alive and still useless: deadlocked, out of connections, or failing every request. The check probes real behaviour, and orchestrators use the result: Compose's `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` waits for it, and Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes stop routing to, or restart, what fails. Plain Docker only marks the container unhealthy.
explain_choice: Ports are published with EXPOSE and -p, which say nothing about whether the service answers correctly.
The result shows in docker ps and inspect, but its purpose is to drive decisions, not to decorate the logs.
Restarting on exit is the restart policy's job; a health check catches the process that is still running but not working.

questions.prompt: How should a database password reach a production container?
choices: Copied in as a .env file, then deleted again in a later build layer
As a Dockerfile ARG, since build arguments are not kept in the image
Injected at run time, as a mounted secret or an environment variable
Hardcoded in the code, but pushed to a private registry that few can pull
questions.explain: Image layers are immutable archives that anyone who can pull the image can unpack, so a secret written into any layer stays readable even if a later layer deletes it. Supplying it at run time keeps it out of the image entirely; for secrets needed during a build, BuildKit's `RUN --mount=type=secret` avoids writing them into a layer.
explain_choice: Deleting a file in a later layer only hides it; the earlier layer still contains it and can be extracted.
ARG values used by a RUN step show up in docker history, so build arguments leak exactly what you tried to hide.
Private registries get shared, mirrored and leaked; access to the image should not mean access to the database.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason to run CI on every push, not just after merging?
choices: So that developers no longer need to run any tests on their machines
To deploy every commit, so production keeps matching the branch
To replace code review, since a green build means the code is right
To catch a failing test on the branch, before it can reach main
questions.explain: Feedback is cheapest while the change is small and its author still has it in their head. A required status check blocks the merge until tests, lint and type checks pass; a check that only runs after merge reports a problem everyone on main already has.
explain_choice: CI is the backstop, not the loop; running the fast tests locally still gives you answers in seconds instead of minutes.
Continuous deployment is a separate decision; CI's job is to verify, and many teams deploy only tagged releases.
Tests check what someone thought to test; review catches design, naming and missing cases that no build can.

questions.prompt: What does a rollback need in order to work under pressure?
choices: The previous immutable image, plus migrations the old code can tolerate
The :latest tag, pulled again on every host that runs the service
A rebuild from the old git tag, since it produces the same image
A fresh database backup, restored just before you redeploy the old version
questions.explain: Redeploying an artifact that already ran is fast and predictable. The usual blocker is the schema: if the new release dropped or renamed a column, the old code breaks against it. Expand-then-contract migrations (add first, remove only a release later) keep the previous version runnable.
explain_choice: :latest moves with every push, so it points at the release you are trying to get away from.
A rebuild pulls whatever base image and dependency versions exist today, so it is a new, untested artifact.
Restoring a backup throws away every write since it was taken; it is disaster recovery, not a rollback.

questions.prompt: An endpoint checks that you are logged in, but not that invoice 1043 is yours. Which OWASP risk is this?
choices: Injection, because the invoice id is taken straight from the URL
Broken access control: an insecure direct object reference
Security misconfiguration of the web server's default settings
Broken authentication, because the login check itself is too weak
questions.explain: Authentication establishes who you are; authorisation must then be checked on every request, for every object, on the server. One endpoint that forgets the ownership check exposes every record behind it, which is why broken access control is A01 in the OWASP Top 10 (2021).
explain_choice: The id is used as data, not code; nothing is injected, the server simply never asks who owns the record.
No setting is wrong; the missing ownership check is a design flaw in the application's own code.
The login works as intended; the flaw is what the logged-in user is allowed to reach afterwards.

questions.prompt: What actually defends against SQL injection?
choices: Validating the length and type of each input at the API boundary
Escaping every quote character in the input before building the string
Parameterised queries, so the values travel separately from the SQL text itself
Rejecting any input that contains SQL keywords such as DROP or UNION
questions.explain: With placeholders, the database parses the statement before the values are bound, so no value can change the query's structure. Escaping and keyword filters try to predict every dangerous input, and attackers get unlimited tries at the gap (numeric contexts, encodings, comments). Identifiers such as table names cannot be parameters, so allowlist those.
explain_choice: Validation narrows the input and is worth doing, but a valid-looking string can still carry SQL if it is concatenated.
Escaping misses contexts where no quote is needed, such as `WHERE id = 1 OR 1=1`, and is easy to forget in one place.
Keyword blocklists break real input (a user called Union) and are bypassed with case, comments or encodings.

questions.prompt: Your server fetches any URL a user supplies. What is the main risk?
choices: SSRF: requests sent from inside your network to your internal services
Mostly slow responses, which a strict timeout on every fetch will handle
CSRF: the fetch riding on your users' own logged-in browser sessions
XSS: the fetched page's scripts running in your other users' browsers
questions.explain: The request leaves from your server's network position, so it can reach what the attacker cannot: cloud metadata at 169.254.169.254, admin panels, databases on private addresses. Defend with an allowlist of destinations, resolve the host and check the IP before connecting (DNS rebinding), and do not follow redirects blindly.
explain_choice: A timeout limits how long a request can hang, not where it can go; an internal metadata call answers in milliseconds.
CSRF abuses a victim's browser and cookies; here the server makes the request with its own network access.
XSS needs the fetched content rendered into a page for users; the fetch itself is dangerous even if nothing is shown.

questions.prompt: What is rate limiting on a login endpoint mainly for?
choices: Stopping a botnet that spreads its attempts over thousands of addresses
Cutting the CPU spent on slow password hashes during busy periods
Protecting users from locking themselves out with wrong passwords
Making brute force and credential stuffing too slow to be worth it
questions.explain: Credential stuffing replays leaked username and password pairs, and brute force guesses; both need huge numbers of attempts, so throttling per account and per IP removes their economics. A distributed attack stays under per-IP limits, so pair throttling with MFA, breached-password checks and alerts on failure spikes.
explain_choice: A botnet spread over many addresses stays under per-IP limits, which is why throttling alone does not detect it.
It does save some hashing work, but that is a side effect; the goal is to deny attackers the volume of guesses they need.
Lockouts come from failed attempts, and rate limiting does nothing to prevent a user mistyping their own password.
