questions.prompt: A dependency audit flags a known CVE in one of your packages. What is the right first step?
choices: Check whether your code reaches the vulnerable path, then plan the upgrade
Nothing, as long as your own code does not import the affected module directly
Pin the current version, so that nothing changes under you while you look
Fork the library and patch the vulnerable function in your own copy
questions.explain: Reachability decides urgency: a flaw in code you call with untrusted input needs a same-day fix or mitigation, one in an unused feature can ride the next release. Either way you upgrade, because the next change to your code may make it reachable. Tools such as pip-audit check transitive dependencies too.
explain_choice: Transitive dependencies run inside your process too; a library you import may call the vulnerable code for you.
Pinning freezes the vulnerable version in place; it stops accidental change but also stops the fix.
A private fork cuts you off from every later upstream security fix, which is usually worse than the original CVE.

questions.prompt: What should security logging capture?
choices: Errors alone, since successful requests are not security events
Full request bodies, so that any incident can be replayed exactly later
Logins, access denials and admin actions, with no secrets or tokens
No user identifiers at all, so the logs hold nothing sensitive
questions.explain: An investigation reconstructs who did what, when and from where, so the events that matter are authentication, authorisation failures and privileged changes, each tied to a user and a request id. Logs are copied widely and kept for a long time, so a logged password or token turns the log store into a breach of its own.
explain_choice: A successful login from a new country, or an admin granting rights, is often the breach; logging only errors misses it.
Request bodies contain passwords, tokens and personal data; logging them makes every log reader a potential attacker.
Without who did it, a log cannot answer the first question of any investigation; minimise data, do not remove identity.

questions.prompt: What is a prompt injection in an LLM-based system?
choices: A chat-box problem, which goes away if users are not allowed free text
Untrusted text the model reads steering it into actions you did not intend
Malicious code slipped into the prompt template when the app is built
A user talking the model out of its safety training with a cleverly worded prompt
questions.explain: The model cannot reliably tell instructions from data, so a web page, email or tool result it reads can carry commands that it then follows with your application's permissions. Treat all such content as untrusted input, and put real permission checks in front of any tool with side effects rather than relying on the prompt.
explain_choice: Indirect injection comes through retrieved documents, emails and tool output, with no attacker ever typing in the chat.
Tampering with the template is a supply-chain problem; injection arrives at run time in content the model reads.
That is a jailbreak, aimed at the model's own rules; injection hijacks your application through content it processes.

questions.prompt: What does defence in depth mean?
choices: Keeping the architecture secret, so attackers have nothing to plan with
One control made strong enough that it needs no backup behind it
Encrypting data at every layer, both at rest and in transit
Several independent controls, so one failure is not a breach
questions.explain: Every control eventually fails through a bug, a misconfiguration or a stolen credential, so the design question is what still stands when one does. Independence matters: controls that share a failure cause, such as one leaked admin key, count as one layer.
explain_choice: Obscurity delays an attacker at best; once the design leaks, nothing is left, so it cannot be the strategy.
No single control survives every bug and misconfiguration; betting everything on one turns its first failure into a breach.
Encryption is one useful layer, but it does nothing against a request the application wrongly authorises.

questions.prompt: Which systems may you run security tests against?
choices: Any site with a bug bounty, whatever its stated scope says
Any public site, provided you report whatever you find
Only systems you own, or have written permission to test
Any system at all, provided you cause no damage or downtime
questions.explain: Unauthorised access is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions (the Computer Misuse Act in the UK, the CFAA in the US) regardless of intent or harm. Written authorisation with a defined scope is what separates a security test from an attack.
explain_choice: A bounty's scope is the permission; testing outside it is unauthorised, bounty or not.
Good intentions and a report afterwards do not create permission; the access itself is the offence.
Harm is not the test; merely accessing a system without authorisation is illegal in most places.

quizzes.name: AI engineering
quizzes.desc: Models from scratch, and systems around them.

questions.prompt: What does backpropagation compute?
choices: Numerical gradients, by nudging each weight and re-running the net
The loss, by running the network from its output back to its input
The updated weights, by stepping each one against its gradient
The gradient of the loss for every parameter, by the chain rule
questions.explain: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation walks the computation graph from the loss back to the inputs, multiplying each node's local derivative by the gradient flowing in from above. One backward pass yields every parameter's gradient; a separate optimiser step (SGD, Adam) then decides how to change the weights.
explain_choice: Nudging each weight is finite differences, useful for checking gradients but one full pass per parameter, far too slow to train with.
The loss comes from the forward pass; the backward pass starts from that loss and computes derivatives.
Changing the weights is the optimiser's job; backprop only supplies the gradients it uses.

questions.prompt: A layer's gradients are zero for almost every unit. What is the usual cause?
choices: The learning rate is too high, so every update overshoots past the minimum
The loss has reached zero, so there is nothing left for it to correct
Saturated activations or dead ReLUs, so that layer has stopped learning
Training has converged, and the layer has reached its best weights
questions.explain: A saturated sigmoid or tanh has a local derivative near zero, and a ReLU whose pre-activation is negative has exactly zero, so the chain rule multiplies that layer's gradient down to nothing. Plot activation and gradient histograms per layer, as Karpathy's lectures do; the fix is usually better initialisation, normalisation or a lower learning rate.
explain_choice: Too high a learning rate usually shows as a loss that jumps or diverges, although large updates can push ReLUs into the dead region.
A zero training loss is rare and would zero every layer, not one; one silent layer points at that layer's activations.
A converged model still has noisy, non-zero gradients from each batch; exactly zero across a layer means units are switched off.

questions.prompt: You fit a StandardScaler on the whole dataset, then split it into train and test. What is wrong?
choices: The test set ends up too small to give a reliable estimate of accuracy
Test-set statistics leaked into training, so the test score is optimistic
Nothing, because scaling does not look at the labels, so there is nothing to leak
The model will now overfit, because scaling adds new features to learn
questions.explain: The scaler's mean and variance were computed partly from test rows, so the training data already reflects the test distribution and the evaluation no longer imitates unseen data. Split first, fit every preprocessing step on the training fold only, and put the steps in a Pipeline so cross-validation refits them per fold.
explain_choice: The split sizes are the same either way; the problem is what information crossed the split, not how big it is.
Leakage does not need labels; any statistic computed from test rows gives the model information it will not have in production.
Standard scaling changes each feature's range; it adds no features and does not change model capacity.

questions.prompt: A fraud model scores 99% accuracy on data where 1% of cases are fraud. What does that tell you?
choices: Almost nothing: always predicting 'not fraud' also scores 99%
That it is ready to ship, since anything above 95% counts as strong
That the data needs more fraud rows before it can be trained
That the model catches about 99 per cent of the fraud cases
questions.explain: Accuracy counts every correct prediction equally, so on imbalanced data the majority class dominates the score. Recall (how much fraud you catch) and precision (how many alerts are real), or the area under the precision-recall curve, measure the thing you care about.
explain_choice: No accuracy threshold means anything without the base rate; here 99% is the score of doing nothing.
More fraud rows might help later, but the question is what the score says, and it says almost nothing.
That is recall, which accuracy does not report; the model could catch no fraud at all and still score 99%.

questions.prompt: In self-attention, how does each token build its output?
choices: By adding its own position in the sequence to its token embedding
As a weighted mix of the value vectors of the tokens it attends to
By picking the single most relevant token and copying its vector
By reading the hidden state of the token immediately before it
questions.explain: Each token's query is compared with every key by a dot product, scaled by the square root of the key size, and softmaxed into weights that sum to one; those weights mix the value vectors. The query, key and value projections are learned, so the model learns what to look for, and a causal mask stops a decoder attending to future tokens.
explain_choice: Adding position is the positional encoding, which happens before attention so the model knows token order.
Softmax gives soft weights over all positions; copying one token would be hard attention, which is not differentiable.
Reading only the previous step is how a recurrent network passes information; attention can reach any allowed position directly.

questions.prompt: A RAG system gives a poor answer. Where does the fault most often lie?
choices: Retrieval: the passage with the answer never reached the model
The temperature: setting it lower would stop the hallucination
The prompt: longer instructions fix most wrong answers alone
The model: a larger one would simply have known the answer anyway
questions.explain: Generation can only use what is in the context window, and chunking, embeddings and ranking decide what gets there. Log the retrieved chunks for every answer and measure recall at k on labelled questions; if the right passage is not in the top results, no prompt or model change will fix it.
explain_choice: Lower temperature makes the output more predictable, not better informed; it will confidently repeat the wrong context.
Instructions cannot supply facts the model was never given; prompt changes help only once retrieval is right.
The point of RAG is answering from your documents, which no model memorised; a bigger model without the passage still guesses.

questions.prompt: What is an evaluation set for in an AI system?
choices: Tuning the prompt until every case in the set passes
Showing stakeholders one headline score per release
Telling whether a change helped, and catching regressions
Giving the model more labelled examples to learn from later
questions.explain: A fixed set of labelled cases turns 'it seems better' into a score you can compare before and after each change, and a case that used to pass and now fails flags a regression before users find it. It is held out from training and from prompt-fitting, so it measures generalisation rather than memory.
explain_choice: Optimising against the eval set overfits to it; the score rises while real-world quality does not.
A summary number is a by-product; the value is comparing changes and spotting regressions case by case.
Examples you train on stop measuring anything; evaluation data must stay out of training to stay honest.

questions.prompt: What does setting temperature to 0 give you?
choices: Identical output on every call, which the API guarantees at zero
Shorter answers, because the model stops sampling tokens at an earlier point
Factually correct answers, because the randomness has been removed
Near-deterministic picks of the likeliest token, not always correct ones
questions.explain: Temperature rescales the logits before sampling, and at zero the most probable token is always taken (greedy decoding). The most probable continuation of a mistaken belief is still mistaken. Hosted APIs can still vary slightly at zero because batching and floating-point order change the arithmetic, so do not build on exact repeatability.
explain_choice: Batched inference and floating-point ordering can still change the output between calls, so zero is not a guarantee.
Length is set by the model's stop token and by max_tokens, not by temperature.
Correctness depends on what the model knows and what is in the context; greedy decoding just picks its favourite wrong answer.

questions.prompt: What does a text embedding encode?
choices: Word counts for each term, like a bag-of-words vector with weights
The exact words, so the original text can be decoded back out of it
Meaning as a position in space, so similar texts sit close together
The key terms in the text, so exact-match search becomes more precise
questions.explain: An embedding model maps text to a dense vector trained so that texts used in similar ways land near each other, measured by cosine similarity. That is why vector search finds paraphrases keyword search misses, and why it can miss exact identifiers such as error codes, which is what hybrid search with BM25 recovers.
explain_choice: Bag-of-words vectors are sparse term counts; dense embeddings capture meaning, so 'car' and 'automobile' end up close.
Embeddings are lossy; many different texts map to nearby vectors and the original wording is not stored.
Exact-match search is what embeddings are weak at; keyword indexes such as BM25 handle it better.

questions.prompt: What must be in place before you give an LLM agent tools with side effects?
choices: Permission checks, argument validation, and all tool output treated as untrusted
A larger, more capable model, since better models do not misuse tools
A system prompt that tells the model clearly which tools not to misuse
Freedom to call any tool at all, with the logs reviewed afterwards for misuse
questions.explain: An agent that can act is an API client whose requests are written by a model that injected text can steer. Controls therefore have to sit in code the model cannot talk its way past: scoped permissions, validated arguments, confirmation for irreversible actions, and treating every tool result as data rather than instructions.
explain_choice: Capability does not stop injection; a stronger model follows injected instructions just as well.
A prompt is a request to the model, not a control; injected text can override it.
Logs tell you afterwards what went wrong; a deleted database or a sent email cannot be taken back by reading them.

questions.prompt: With at-least-once delivery, a consumer receives the same message twice. What must it do?
choices: Nothing; the broker filters out duplicates before they are delivered
Recognise or absorb the repeat, so the second copy changes nothing
Process it again in full, since the first attempt may have failed
Reject it, so the broker moves the copy to the dead-letter queue
questions.explain: Duplicates come from the gap between doing the work and acknowledging it: if the ack is lost or the worker dies after the side effect, the broker redelivers. Consumers either record processed message ids alongside the effect, or make the operation naturally idempotent (an upsert, 'set status to paid') so a repeat is harmless.
explain_choice: At-least-once means the broker cannot know the first delivery succeeded, so it deliberately redelivers; deduplication is your job.
If the first attempt succeeded, a full second run repeats its side effects, such as a second email or a second charge.
A duplicate is not a failure; dead-lettering it would bury a valid message and still leave the first copy's effect in place.

questions.prompt: What goes into a dead-letter queue?
choices: A copy of every single message, kept as an audit log of the main queue
Messages that expired unread, kept for a day and then deleted
Duplicate deliveries that the broker has already filtered out
Messages that kept failing, parked for inspection and later replay
questions.explain: After a set number of failed attempts, a poison message is moved aside so it stops blocking or endlessly retrying at the head of the queue. Someone then inspects it, fixes the bug or the data, and replays it; without a DLQ it either jams the queue or is dropped with no trace.
explain_choice: An audit trail is a different design; a DLQ holds only the failures, which is what makes it useful to inspect.
Some brokers can dead-letter expired messages too, but the core use is repeated processing failure, and nothing deletes them automatically.
Brokers with at-least-once delivery do not filter duplicates; the consumer has to.

questions.prompt: Why is cache invalidation hard?
choices: Deleting a key is a slow operation in most cache servers, such as Redis
Serialising objects into the cache loses their types, so reads go wrong
The cache cannot see writes that bypass it, so it cannot tell when it has gone stale
Memory limits evict entries long before they ever get a chance to go stale
questions.explain: Staleness is a fact about the source of truth, and the cache only learns of it if something tells it. Races make even explicit deletes unreliable: a reader can fetch old data, the writer updates and deletes the key, then the reader stores its old copy. TTLs bound how long staleness can last; event-based invalidation tightens it at the cost of coupling.
explain_choice: Deletes in Redis or Memcached are fast; the difficulty is knowing when to delete and ordering it against concurrent reads.
Serialisation is a solved, local problem; it does not explain why cached data drifts away from the database.
Eviction removes entries under memory pressure but does nothing for a hot entry that stays cached while its data changes.

questions.prompt: What must a web service do before you can run many copies behind a load balancer?
choices: Keep no per-user state in process memory, using a shared store instead
Be packaged in containers, since containers are what get replicated
Run on bigger machines, so that each copy can handle more of the traffic
Use sticky sessions, so each user keeps returning to the same instance
questions.explain: Any instance must be able to serve any request, and instances must be free to die or be added. Sessions, uploads and caches kept in local memory break that, so they move to Redis, a database or object storage, and the instances become interchangeable.
explain_choice: Any process can be replicated; containers make deployment easier but do not make a stateful service stateless.
Bigger machines are vertical scaling; horizontal scaling adds more copies, which only works if they are interchangeable.
Sticky sessions work until that instance dies or you scale down, then its users lose their state; they hide the problem.

questions.prompt: Why is a distributed lock with an expiry time still risky?
choices: Locks do not work across machines, just between threads in one process
Redis is single-threaded, so every lock call queues behind others
Expiry slows every holder down, since each one must keep renewing
A holder can pause past its lease, so two workers may act at once
questions.explain: A GC pause, a slow disk or a network partition can outlast the lease; the lock expires, another worker takes it, and the first wakes up still believing it holds it. A lock that never expires deadlocks when its holder dies, so the safe design adds a fencing token (an increasing number) that the storage checks on every write.
explain_choice: Distributed locks do work across machines; the problem is that clocks and failure detection there are unreliable.
Redis handles lock calls in microseconds; the danger is correctness under pauses, not throughput.
Renewing a lease is a cheap background call; the real danger is a paused holder whose lease lapses while it still acts.

questions.prompt: What does distributed tracing tell you that logs alone do not?
choices: Everything logs and metrics do, so it can replace both of them
How one request's spans connect across services, and their timings
The outcome of every single request, whereas log lines tend to be sampled
More detail about each event than a single log line can hold
questions.explain: Each span carries a trace id propagated through headers and message metadata, so spans from the API, the queue and the worker join into one tree with parent-child timing. That shows where the time went along the whole path, which scattered log lines from separate services cannot.
explain_choice: Traces are usually sampled and are poor for counting; metrics answer 'how many', logs answer 'what exactly'.
It is the other way round: logs are usually complete and traces are commonly sampled to control cost.
Spans carry some attributes, but log lines can hold as much detail as you like; the difference is the causal link.

questions.prompt: What does durable execution, in the style of Temporal, mainly give you?
choices: Faster workflows, because each of the steps runs in parallel by default
Cheaper hosting, because workers can sleep between the steps
Workflow state that survives a worker crash and resumes mid-flight
Exactly-once side effects, so activities need no idempotency
questions.explain: The platform records each step's result in an event history, so when a worker dies another one replays that history and continues from the last completed step instead of starting again. Crash recovery moves out of your business code, which is where it is usually done badly.
explain_choice: Steps run in the order the workflow code says; parallelism is something you write explicitly.
Cost is not the point; waiting steps are cheap because state is persisted, but workers still run all the time.
Activities are retried at least once, so an activity that sends email or charges a card still has to be idempotent.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between cache-aside and write-through caching?
choices: Cache-aside fills the cache on a read miss; write-through updates it on each write
Cache-aside does not go stale, while write-through is stale until a TTL expires
Write-through caches just the reads, while cache-aside caches both the reads and the writes
They differ in where the cache runs, not in when it gets filled or updated
questions.explain: In cache-aside the application reads the cache, and on a miss loads from the database and stores the result, so only data someone asked for is cached, but entries stay stale until a TTL or an explicit delete. In write-through every write goes through the cache to the store, keeping cached entries fresh at the cost of slower writes and caching data that may never be read.
explain_choice: It is roughly the reverse: cache-aside entries go stale after the database changes, while write-through updates them on each write.
Write-through is defined by what happens on writes; cache-aside does not touch the cache on writes except to delete.
Both can use the same cache server; the patterns differ in when data enters the cache and who keeps it fresh.

questions.prompt: What should an architecture decision record contain?
choices: A diagram of the final design, edited whenever the design changes
The option you chose, plus the code that implements it in full
Every option, re-scored from scratch whenever requirements change
The context, the options you rejected, and why you rejected them
questions.explain: An ADR preserves the reasoning, not just the outcome: the forces at the time, what was considered and what was traded away. When the context changes you write a new ADR that supersedes the old one, so the history shows why each decision made sense when it was made, and the same debate does not restart every six months.
explain_choice: ADRs are immutable once accepted; a change of design gets a new record that supersedes the old one.
The code shows what was built, not why; the rejected options and the reasons are what a later reader cannot recover.
Re-scoring in place erases the original reasoning; a new superseding record keeps both decisions visible.

questions.prompt: Your order logic imports the Postgres client directly. What does applying dependency inversion at that boundary change?
choices: The Postgres client is wrapped in a class that exposes exactly the same methods
The order logic and the database are split into two separate microservices
The logic depends on an interface it owns, which a Postgres adapter implements
Postgres now calls into the order logic, instead of the logic calling Postgres
questions.explain: Inversion is about the direction of source dependencies: the core defines the interface in its own terms (save_order, find_order) and the infrastructure depends on the core, not the other way round. Tests can then use an in-memory fake, and replacing the store touches only the adapter.
explain_choice: A thin wrapper that mirrors the client's API still ties the logic to Postgres concepts; the interface must speak the domain's language.
Splitting into services is a deployment decision; the same inversion applies inside one process.
Control flow still goes from logic to database at run time; what flips is which side the code depends on.

questions.prompt: A worker acknowledges each message as soon as it receives it, then processes it. What delivery guarantee does that give?
choices: At-most-once: a crash during processing loses the message
Exactly-once, because each message is acknowledged just once
At-least-once: the broker redelivers it if the worker crashes
It depends on the broker's settings alone, not on the ack timing
questions.explain: Once acknowledged, the broker deletes the message, so if the worker dies mid-job nobody will ever process it. Acknowledging after the work is done flips this to at-least-once: nothing is lost, but a crash between the work and the ack causes a redelivery, which is why consumers must be idempotent.
explain_choice: One ack per message says nothing about whether the work happened; acking first means the work can be lost.
Redelivery only happens for messages that were never acknowledged; here the ack has already been sent.
The broker's guarantee is only as good as when the consumer acknowledges; ack placement decides the outcome.

questions.prompt: A gateway makes up to three attempts at an API, and the API makes up to three attempts at its database. The database slows down. What happens?
choices: Retries smooth out the spike, because each one waits for its backoff first
One client request can become nine database calls, deepening the overload
The gateway's retries are absorbed by the API's own retries, so load is flat
Load stays about the same, because a failed call does no work on the database
questions.explain: Attempts multiply at each layer that retries, so a slowdown at the bottom triggers a storm aimed at the part that is already struggling. Retry at one layer only, cap retries with a retry budget or circuit breaker, and add jittered backoff so clients do not retry in step.
explain_choice: Backoff spaces out each client's retries, but every retry still arrives; it spreads the extra load rather than removing it.
Each gateway attempt starts a fresh set of API attempts; the layers multiply, they do not cancel out.
A call that timed out often ran to completion on the database anyway, so every retry adds real work.

questions.prompt: A consumer inserts an order row, then separately marks the message id as processed. It crashes between the two. What fixes this?
choices: Turn on the broker's exactly-once mode, so it stops redelivering
Retry the order insert in a loop until the database finally accepts it
Mark the id as processed first, then insert the order afterwards
Write the order and the processed id in one database transaction
questions.explain: Two separate writes always leave a window where one has happened and the other has not, and a crash in that window leaves the record and the effect disagreeing. Committing both atomically means redelivery sees the id and skips, which is 'effectively once': no system delivers exactly once, but the outcome can be made to look like it.
explain_choice: Brokers cannot see your database, so they cannot know whether your side effect happened; redelivery is still possible.
Retrying the insert does nothing for the crash window; on redelivery the order would be inserted twice.
Reversing the order moves the window: a crash now leaves the id marked and the order never written, so it is lost.

questions.prompt: A user saves a new display name, and the next page still shows the old one. Reads go to a replica. Which guarantee is missing?
choices: Durability of the committed write
Read-your-writes consistency
Atomicity of the update
Availability of the primary
questions.explain: With asynchronous replication a replica lags the primary, so a read straight after a write can miss it even though the write is safe. Read-your-writes is usually restored by sending that user's reads to the primary for a short while, or by waiting until the replica has caught up to the write's position.
explain_choice: The write is committed on the primary and will reach the replica; nothing was lost, it has just not arrived yet.
The update applied in full; the replica simply shows an older, complete version.
The primary accepted the write, so it was available; the stale read came from a lagging replica.

questions.prompt: Your call to the payment service times out. What do you know about the payment?
choices: Nothing yet: it may have succeeded, failed, or still be running
It was rolled back, because the client closed the connection
It succeeded, since a timeout affects just the response
It failed, since a timeout means the request did not arrive at all
questions.explain: In a distributed system a timeout is the absence of an answer, not an answer: the request may have been lost, processed with the reply lost, or still be in progress. Resolve it by querying the payment's status or retrying with the same idempotency key, never by assuming either outcome.
explain_choice: Remote services do not roll back because a client stopped waiting; the work usually carries on.
It might have succeeded, but a lost request produces exactly the same timeout, so you cannot assume it.
The request may well have arrived and been processed; only the reply is missing.

questions.prompt: Why not add user_id as a label on a request-latency metric?
choices: Metric systems store numeric labels alone, so string ids like these are rejected outright
Labels on metrics are dropped after an hour, so the per-user detail is wasted
Each distinct label value creates a new time series, so storage and queries blow up
Per-user labels distort the histogram, so the reported percentiles become wrong
questions.explain: A metrics backend stores one series per unique combination of label values, so a million users means a million series for one metric, which exhausts memory and makes queries slow. Keep metric labels to small, bounded sets (route, status) and put per-user detail in logs and traces, where high cardinality is cheap.
explain_choice: Label values are strings in Prometheus and OpenTelemetry; the problem is how many distinct values there are, not their type.
Retention applies to whole series; nothing drops labels, which is why the cost keeps growing.
The histograms stay accurate per series; the issue is the number of series, not the maths inside each one.

questions.prompt: Why must Temporal workflow code avoid calling random() or reading the system clock directly?
choices: The SDK blocks system calls inside workflows for security reasons alone
Recovery replays the event history, and the replay must take exactly the same path
Workflows run on several workers at once, which must share the same seed
Random values and timestamps do not serialise into the event history cleanly
questions.explain: When a worker resumes a workflow it re-runs the workflow code against the recorded history and expects the same decisions in the same order. A different random value or timestamp on replay sends the code down a new branch that does not match the history, so the SDK provides deterministic versions (workflow.now(), workflow.random()) and anything non-deterministic belongs in an activity, whose result is recorded.
explain_choice: The restriction is about determinism, not security; activities may call anything they like.
A workflow execution runs on one worker at a time; the issue is replaying later, not running in parallel.
Numbers and timestamps serialise easily; the history records them when they come from the SDK's own deterministic calls.

questions.prompt: Queue depth has climbed steadily all afternoon, and every worker reports healthy. What does that tell you?
choices: The broker is slow to deliver, so the workers are idle
Nothing yet; depth matters once messages start to expire
One worker must be stuck, since healthy workers keep up
Messages arrive faster than the workers finish them
questions.explain: Depth grows whenever the arrival rate exceeds the processing rate, even with every worker working correctly. By Little's law, waiting time is roughly depth divided by throughput, so a rising queue means rising latency. Adding workers helps only if the bottleneck is the workers and not the database behind them, so check that first.
explain_choice: An idle worker pool with a growing queue would be a delivery problem, but healthy busy workers point to capacity.
Every queued message is a user waiting; latency grows with depth long before anything expires.
Healthy workers can still be too few or too slow for the load; health says they work, not that they keep up.

questions.prompt: How does CPython reclaim most objects?
choices: Reference counting frees each one when its count reaches zero
It is released when the function that made it returns
A tracing collector sweeps the whole heap every so often, as in Java
Objects stay allocated until you call `del` or `gc.collect()` yourself
questions.explain: Every object carries a count of the references to it; each binding, container slot or argument adds one and each removal subtracts one, so an object is freed at the exact moment the last reference goes. The cyclic collector runs only occasionally, and exists solely for groups of objects that refer to each other and so never reach zero.
explain_choice: Python values live on the heap, not in the call's stack frame, so a returned or stored object outlives the function that made it.
That is how the JVM and .NET work; CPython keeps a tracing pass only for reference cycles, not for ordinary objects.
`del` removes one name, not the object, and `gc.collect()` only looks for cycles; ordinary objects die as soon as their count hits zero.

questions.prompt: After `a = [1, 2, 3]` and then `b = a`, what has happened to the list?
choices: `b` holds a deep copy, so changing `b[0]` leaves `a` untouched
The count is unchanged, since both names share the very same object
No copy is made; only the list's reference count goes up by one
`b` holds a shallow copy, so there are now two lists of refcount one
questions.explain: Assignment binds a name to an existing object; it never copies. Binding a second name stores another pointer to the same PyObject and increments its ob_refcnt, which is why `b.append(4)` is visible through `a`. The count only returns to its old value when one name is rebound or deleted.
explain_choice: Deep copies come only from `copy.deepcopy`; here both names reach one list, so a change through `b` shows through `a`.
Sharing one object is exactly what a reference is, and each new reference is counted; that count is how CPython knows when the list can be freed.
Only `a[:]`, `list(a)` or `copy.copy(a)` make a new list; a plain assignment never does.

questions.prompt: How does CPython run a `.py` file?
choices: It interprets the source text line by line, reparsing each line it reaches
It compiles the source to bytecode, then an interpreter loop runs that
It compiles every function to native machine code before running it
It translates the file to C and builds it with the system's C compiler
questions.explain: The whole module is parsed and compiled to a code object before any of it runs, which is why a syntax error on the last line stops the first line running. The evaluation loop then executes that bytecode instruction by instruction, specialising hot instructions since 3.11; `dis.dis` shows the result and `.pyc` files cache it.
explain_choice: A syntax error anywhere in a file stops all of it running, which proves the whole file is compiled before execution starts.
The JIT added in 3.13 is experimental and off by default in 3.14; standard CPython runs bytecode in its interpreter loop.
That describes Cython, a separate tool; CPython itself never produces or compiles C from your code.

questions.prompt: Why is a NumPy array operation such as `a * 2` so much faster than a Python loop?
choices: It caches results, so repeating a calculation is free
NumPy spreads every array operation across all of your CPU cores
NumPy's own Python code is compiled with far heavier optimisation
One C loop runs over a packed, single-type buffer of raw numbers
questions.explain: A Python list holds pointers to separate boxed objects, so each step of a loop must dispatch on type, unbox, compute and allocate a new object. A NumPy array is one contiguous block of fixed-type values, so a single compiled loop does the arithmetic with no per-element interpreter work, and can use SIMD. A Python-level loop over the array puts that per-element overhead straight back.
explain_choice: NumPy does no memoisation; `a * 2` computed twice does the full work twice.
Most element-wise operations run on one core; only some routines, such as BLAS-backed matrix products, use threads.
The speed comes from compiled C over typed memory, not from any special handling of NumPy's Python code.

questions.prompt: Two objects refer to each other and nothing else refers to either. What eventually frees them?
choices: Nothing; CPython leaks every cycle until the process finally exits
The cyclic garbage collector, on one of its later passes
Reference counting, as soon as the last outside name is deleted
The `del` statement, provided you apply it to both of the objects
questions.explain: Each object still holds a reference to the other, so neither count can reach zero and reference counting alone never frees them. The collector periodically finds container objects reachable only from each other and breaks the cycle. Because that runs later rather than immediately, large cyclic structures linger; `weakref` back-references or explicit unlinking avoid creating the cycle at all.
explain_choice: The `gc` module exists precisely to find these; cycles are reclaimed, just later than ordinary objects.
Each object's count stays at one because the other still points at it, so reference counting never gets to zero.
`del` only removes names; the objects still point at each other, so their counts stay above zero until the collector runs.

questions.prompt: What does the free-threaded CPython build (`python3.14t`) change?
choices: Threads can run Python bytecode in parallel, with no GIL
Nothing supported yet: like the JIT, it is still an experiment
asyncio coroutines now run on several CPU cores without any changes
Single-threaded code runs faster, since it no longer takes a lock
questions.explain: PEP 703 replaced the GIL with per-object locking and biased reference counting so that threads can run bytecode on separate cores at once; PEP 779 made the build officially supported in 3.14, though not the default. The price is some single-threaded overhead and C extensions that must declare themselves safe, or importing one turns the GIL back on. The JIT is a separate project and remains experimental.
explain_choice: Free-threading moved from experimental to supported in 3.14 (PEP 779); it is the JIT that is still experimental.
asyncio still runs its coroutines on one thread per event loop; removing the GIL helps threads, not coroutines.
Per-object locking and atomic reference counts make single-threaded code somewhat slower, not faster.

questions.prompt: When is a C extension, or a Rust module built with PyO3, worth its cost?
choices: When the program is slow because it spends its time on network calls
Whenever a module grows big enough to be slow to import
When a profiled hot path dominates runtime and can't be vectorised
As soon as any loop in the code runs more than a million iterations
questions.explain: Native code only pays off where the interpreter's per-operation overhead is the bottleneck, and only a profile tells you where that is. It brings a build toolchain, platform wheels, memory-safety risks and harder debugging, so first try better algorithms or NumPy-style vectorisation, and keep the benchmark that justified the switch.
explain_choice: Waiting on I/O costs the same in C as in Python; concurrency or batching helps, native code does not.
Import time is dominated by what a module does at load, and native code rarely fixes that; profile `python -X importtime` first.
Iteration count alone says nothing; a million cheap iterations may take milliseconds, and vectorising may beat C anyway.

questions.prompt: A list's buffer is full and you call `append`. What happens in memory?
choices: Every element object is duplicated into the newly allocated buffer
The whole list object moves to a new address, so `id(lst)` changes
A linked node is chained on the end, so nothing needs to be copied
A bigger pointer array is allocated and the pointers copied; `id(lst)` stays
questions.explain: A list is a fixed header pointing at a separate array of PyObject pointers. When that array is full, CPython reallocates it with about an eighth of spare room and copies the pointers, not the objects; the header, and so `id()`, never moves. The occasional O(n) copy spread over many cheap appends is what makes append amortised O(1).
explain_choice: The array holds pointers, so only pointers are copied; the element objects are shared and never duplicated.
Only the internal pointer array is reallocated; the list object itself stays put, so its `id()` is stable for its lifetime.
CPython lists are dynamic arrays, not linked lists, which is why indexing is O(1) and growth needs an occasional copy.

questions.prompt: On Python 3.12+, `sys.getrefcount(None)` returns a huge number that doesn't move as you add references. Why?
choices: getrefcount misses references held in C, so it returns an estimate
None is immortal: its count is pinned and increments are skipped
So much code refers to None that the true count really is that high
None lives outside the heap, so that is its address
questions.explain: PEP 683 (3.12) made objects such as None, True, False, small ints and interned strings immortal: their reference count is set to a sentinel that Py_INCREF and Py_DECREF leave alone, which saves memory writes and lets them be shared safely. The exact value is an implementation detail and has changed between releases, so trace refcounts on a list or instance you created.
explain_choice: getrefcount reads the stored count exactly; for an immortal object that stored value is a fixed sentinel.
The value would then rise as you add names; it does not, because updates to an immortal object's count are skipped.
None is an ordinary heap PyObject; the large figure is a sentinel refcount, not an address.

questions.prompt: In C, given `int a[4]; int *p = a;` what does `p + 1` point to?
choices: Nowhere yet: it holds the value of `a[0]` with one added to it
Nothing valid, since adding to a pointer is undefined behaviour in C
The second byte of `a[0]`, one byte on from where `p` points now
`a[1]`, which sits `sizeof(int)` bytes past the start of the array
questions.explain: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type, so `p + 1` advances by one whole `int`; this is exactly why `a[i]` is defined as `*(a + i)`. Adding to a pointer is well-defined while the result stays within the array or one past its end.
explain_choice: That is `*p + 1`, which dereferences first; `p + 1` is still an address.
Arithmetic within an array, and to one past its end, is defined; only going beyond that is undefined.
Only a `char *` steps one byte at a time; the step is always the size of the type the pointer points to.

questions.prompt: A C function returns a pointer to a local array it declared. What goes wrong?
choices: The compiler quietly moves the array to the heap, at a cost in speed
It leaks, because stack memory stays reserved until `free()`
The array lived in that call's stack frame, reclaimed on return
Nothing: the array stays valid until the caller passes it to `free()`
questions.explain: Automatic locals are stored in the function's stack frame, and that space is reused by the next call as soon as the function returns, so the pointer dangles and reading through it is undefined behaviour. Memory that must outlive the call has to come from `malloc` and be freed once by its owner, or be supplied by the caller.
explain_choice: C does no such escape analysis; the frame is simply reclaimed and the pointer dangles.
Stack memory is reclaimed automatically when the function returns; the danger is losing it too early, not leaking it.
`free()` is only for memory from `malloc`; calling it on a stack address is itself undefined behaviour.

questions.prompt: What is a system call?
choices: A request that switches into the kernel to do privileged work like I/O
Any call your program makes into a C library function such as `strlen`
A command the shell runs on your behalf when you type it at a prompt
A call from Python code into a compiled C extension module's function
questions.explain: User programs cannot touch devices, files or other processes directly; a system call traps into the kernel, which checks permission and does the work. Each one costs a mode switch, which is why buffered I/O batches many small writes into few `write` calls, and why `strace` or Process Monitor output explains so much about slow programs.
explain_choice: `strlen` runs entirely in your own process; only functions like `write` or `open` end in a system call.
The shell starts programs using system calls such as fork and exec, but a typed command is not itself one.
Calling an extension is an ordinary function call inside the same process; no kernel is involved.

questions.prompt: Your C files compile cleanly, then the build fails with `undefined reference to 'foo'`. Which stage failed?
choices: Linking: no object file or library given defines `foo`
Loading: the OS couldn't find `foo` when the program started
Compiling: the compiler couldn't parse the call made to `foo`
Preprocessing: the header that declares `foo` was not found
questions.explain: Each file compiles on its own against declarations, leaving calls to outside functions as unresolved symbols. The linker then has to match every symbol with exactly one definition from the object files and libraries it is given, so a missing `.c` file or `-l` flag shows up only at that stage.
explain_choice: A loader failure happens when you run the program; this build never produced a binary to run.
A parse error stops compilation with a syntax message; here every file compiled, so the call itself was understood.
A missing header fails during compilation with 'No such file'; this message comes after compilation succeeded.

questions.prompt: In `dis` output, why does reading a local compile to `LOAD_FAST` but reading a global to `LOAD_GLOBAL`?
choices: LOAD_FAST appears once the first call has cached the value
Both do a dict lookup; the names just record where it was written
Locals are fixed at compile time and sit in indexed frame slots
LOAD_FAST reads a CPU register, while LOAD_GLOBAL goes to memory
questions.explain: The compiler sees every assignment in a function body, so each local gets a numbered slot in the frame and is read by index. A global could be added or rebound at any time, so it needs a lookup in the module's dict and then builtins, which 3.11+ specialises with a cache but which still costs more. 3.14 may show `LOAD_FAST_BORROW`, a variant of the same slot read.
explain_choice: The opcode is chosen at compile time, before any call happens; specialisation later refines it, but it starts as LOAD_FAST.
Only globals are looked up by name; locals are read by position, which is why they are faster.
Both read ordinary memory; the difference is an array index versus a dictionary lookup.

questions.prompt: In CPython, what does every object begin with in memory?
choices: Its raw value, followed by a table listing its method names
A header holding its reference count and a pointer to its type
Nothing for ints and floats, which are stored as bare machine values
A private copy of its class's `__dict__` for fast attribute access
questions.explain: Every object starts with a PyObject header: `ob_refcnt` and `ob_type`, and variable-sized objects add `ob_size`. The type pointer is how the interpreter finds an object's behaviour, including its methods, and the header is why even a small int costs 28 bytes on a 64-bit build.
explain_choice: Methods live once on the type object, reached through `ob_type`; no object stores its own method table.
Unlike Java, CPython has no unboxed primitives; every int and float is a full heap object with a header.
Instances share their class's attributes through the type; copying the class dict into each would waste memory.

questions.prompt: Why did CPython adopt a global interpreter lock in the first place?
choices: asyncio needed it to schedule coroutines safely on its event loop
It makes statements such as `x += 1` atomic, so no lock is needed
So that no two threads can ever run at once, even while blocked on I/O
It made refcount updates and C extensions thread-safe at little cost
questions.explain: Reference counts change on almost every operation, and making each change atomic or locking each object slows single-threaded code. One big lock kept the interpreter and every C extension correct with no fine-grained locking, at the cost of CPU-bound threads never running in parallel. Removing it therefore means per-object locks, atomic or biased counts and extensions audited for thread safety.
explain_choice: The GIL predates asyncio by more than twenty years; an event loop runs on one thread and needs no such lock.
`x += 1` is several bytecodes and a thread switch can land between them; the GIL never made it atomic.
Threads release the GIL during blocking I/O, which is why threads do help I/O-bound programs.

questions.prompt: `timeit` gives several repeat timings. Why is the minimum often a better figure than the mean?
choices: The minimum is the cold-cache time, which is what production code sees
The first repeat compiles the code to C, which skews the mean upward
The mean includes garbage-collection pauses that the minimum filters out
Background noise only ever adds time, so the minimum is least disturbed
questions.explain: Other processes, interrupts and frequency scaling can only slow a run down, never speed it up, so the fastest repeat is the closest to what the code itself costs. That holds for comparing two versions of a small function; for whole programs report a distribution, and always compare on the same inputs and machine.
explain_choice: The fastest repeat is usually the warm-cache one, the opposite of a cold start.
CPython never compiles your code to C; the first repeat may warm caches, but nothing is translated.
`timeit` switches the garbage collector off while timing by default, so there are no GC pauses to filter.

questions.prompt: On the default build, how can a C extension's long loop let other Python threads run meanwhile?
choices: It cannot: C code always holds the GIL until it returns to Python
It starts a subprocess, since threads are unable to share the GIL
It releases the GIL around the loop with `Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS`
The interpreter pre-empts it every 5 ms, as with bytecode
questions.explain: The interpreter only offers to switch threads between bytecode instructions, and a C function is a single call from its point of view. Extension code that does not touch Python objects can release the GIL explicitly and reacquire it before touching them again; NumPy, hashlib and zlib do this, which is why threads can speed them up.
explain_choice: Releasing the GIL is an explicit, documented part of the C API; many libraries depend on it.
Threads share one GIL by taking turns; an extension can hand it back without any extra process.
The switch interval is checked by the bytecode loop, which is not running while C code runs.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes ELT from ETL?
choices: ELT transforms records in Python before they reach any storage
ELT skips transformation and lets analysts query the raw data
ELT streams records in real time, where ETL moves them in batches
Raw data is loaded into the warehouse first and transformed there
questions.explain: Cheap object storage and elastic warehouse compute made it affordable to keep the untouched source data and transform it with SQL inside the warehouse. When the business logic changes you simply rerun the transform over the raw history, which ETL cannot do because it only stored the transformed result.
explain_choice: Transforming before loading is ETL; the letters give the order of the steps.
The transform still happens, in the warehouse, usually as tested SQL models in a tool such as dbt.
Both are usually batch processes; the difference is where and when the transform runs, not how often.

questions.prompt: Why does Parquet usually beat CSV for analytical queries?
choices: It keeps a full index on every column, much like a database table
It is columnar, typed and compressed, so scans skip unused columns
It is row-oriented, so each whole record is read in a single pass
It is plain text, so any tool can stream it without a special parser
questions.explain: Analytical queries usually touch a few columns of many rows. Parquet stores each column contiguously with its type, so similar values compress well and a reader fetches only the columns asked for; row-group min/max statistics also let it skip whole blocks. CSV forces every byte of every row to be read and re-parsed from text.
explain_choice: Parquet keeps min/max statistics per row group, which help skipping, but it has no per-column index like a database.
Row orientation is CSV's layout and suits reading whole records; Parquet is columnar, which suits analytics.
Parquet is binary and needs a library to read; being human-readable is CSV's advantage, not Parquet's.

questions.prompt: A daily job INSERTs yesterday's rows and is retried after a timeout. What makes the rerun safe?
choices: Wrapping the INSERT in a transaction so a second run is rolled back
Removing duplicate rows later in the dashboard query that reads it
Writing with MERGE on a key, or overwriting that day's partition
A retry limit, so the job runs at most three times
questions.explain: A timeout does not tell you whether the first attempt committed, so the rerun must give the same end state either way. An upsert keyed on a natural key, or replacing the whole date partition, makes the write idempotent; a plain INSERT appends a second copy of every row. The same property is what makes backfills safe.
explain_choice: A transaction makes one run all-or-nothing, but a second run is a new transaction that inserts every row again.
Every consumer would then need the same fix, and the stored table stays wrong; correct the data where it is written.
Limiting retries caps how many duplicates you get; it does not stop the second attempt duplicating the first.

questions.prompt: A table is partitioned by `event_date`. Which query gains the most from that?
choices: `WHERE event_date = '2026-09-01'`, as only that day's files are read
A full `COUNT(*)`, since every partition is counted in parallel
Any query at all, since partitioned files compress far better
`WHERE user_id = 42`, since partitions keep rows sorted by each column
questions.explain: Partitioning splits the table into separate directories or files per value, so a filter on the partition column lets the engine prune every other partition before reading a byte. Filters on other columns get no pruning, which is why you partition by the column your heaviest queries filter on.
explain_choice: A full count reads everything regardless; parallelism is available without partitions too, so nothing is pruned.
Partitioning changes which files a query reads, not how well each file compresses.
Partitioning groups rows by one column only; a filter on `user_id` still scans every partition unless the data is also clustered by it.

questions.prompt: Events dated 1 September keep arriving on the 3rd and 4th. What should the pipeline do?
choices: Count them on the day they arrived, so earlier totals stay fixed
Reprocess a trailing window so recent past days can be corrected
Keep every day open until no further events can possibly arrive
Discard them, since the totals for that day are already published
questions.explain: Mobile clients, retries and upstream outages mean event time and arrival time differ. Recomputing the last few days on each run (or using watermarks in streaming) lets totals settle to the right answer, while a bounded window keeps the cost predictable; how many days to reopen is a measured choice.
explain_choice: Booking by arrival time mixes two different days, so both the 1st and the 4th end up wrong.
Some events can arrive arbitrarily late, so a day would never close; a bounded window is the practical compromise.
Dropping late events makes every published total quietly low, which is how dashboards drift away from the source system.

questions.prompt: A not-null test on `order_id` finds 40 nulls. What should happen next?
choices: Replace the nulls with a placeholder so joins still succeed
Log a warning and finish the run so the data stays up to date
Silently drop the 40 bad rows and load all of the others
The run fails before those rows reach any downstream tables
questions.explain: Bad data spreads: once it is loaded, every model and dashboard built on it inherits the defect, and cleaning up costs far more than a delayed run. A failing test stops the spread and forces someone to look; warnings are for checks you would genuinely accept failing.
explain_choice: A placeholder key joins to nothing or to the wrong thing, turning a visible error into a silent one.
Fresh but wrong data is worse than late data, and a warning in a log nobody reads protects nothing.
Silent drops hide an upstream bug and make totals wrong with no trace of why.

questions.prompt: When is moving a job from pandas to Polars or DuckDB most worthwhile?
choices: By default, since pandas has been deprecated in favour of Polars
Once the data outgrows a single machine and needs a cluster
When data nears memory limits or you want lazy, multi-core runs
When you need plotting, since both ship richer charting built in
questions.explain: pandas executes eagerly, mostly on one core, and often copies data. Polars and DuckDB plan the whole query first, push filters and column selection down to the file reader, stream larger-than-memory data and use every core. Beyond one machine is Spark's territory; below it, these two often make a cluster unnecessary.
explain_choice: pandas is actively maintained and fine for small data; the switch is about scale and execution model.
That threshold is where distributed tools like Spark come in; Polars and DuckDB shine on one machine before that.
Neither is a plotting library; both hand data to matplotlib or similar just as pandas does.

questions.prompt: What does an orchestrator such as Airflow or Prefect add over plain cron?
choices: Task dependencies, retries, alerts and a record of every run
Exactly-once delivery for every record that the pipeline moves
Somewhere to store results, so no separate database is needed
Faster execution, because each task is compiled before it runs
questions.explain: Cron only starts a command at a time. An orchestrator models the pipeline as a DAG, so a task waits for its inputs, retries on failure, alerts when it stays broken and records each run for backfills and audits. None of that makes the code faster or the writes idempotent; that is still your job.
explain_choice: Retries can cause duplicates; exactly-once effects come from idempotent task code, not from the scheduler.
The orchestrator's metadata database stores run state, not your data; outputs still go to a warehouse or files.
Orchestrators schedule your code as it is; they do not make individual tasks run any faster.

questions.prompt: A finance report is read once each morning. What does that suggest for the pipeline feeding it?
choices: Either, since batch and streaming cost the same to build and to run
Streaming, because real-time data is more accurate than batch
Batch is enough; streaming costs more for freshness nobody reads
Streaming, because batch jobs are not able to deal with late data
questions.explain: The latency the consumer actually needs decides the architecture. Streaming adds always-on infrastructure, state management and harder reprocessing; if the answer is only looked at once a day, a nightly batch gives the same value at a fraction of the cost and is far easier to backfill.
explain_choice: Streaming needs always-on consumers, state and monitoring, so it costs considerably more to build and run.
Freshness and accuracy are different things; a streaming total can be less accurate while late events are still arriving.
Batch handles late data by reprocessing a trailing window, often more simply than streaming does.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a lakehouse?
choices: A data lake whose files must all be cleaned and saved as CSV
A data warehouse that has been moved onto one on-premises server
A data lake plus a copy of every table loaded into a separate warehouse
Open files in object storage, with a table layer for schema and ACID
questions.explain: A lake is cheap object storage holding files of any shape; a warehouse gives typed tables, SQL and transactions but keeps data in its own store. Table formats such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg add a transaction log and schema over open Parquet files, so one copy of the data serves both roles.
explain_choice: Lakehouses usually hold columnar Parquet, not CSV, and accept semi-structured data too.
Where it is hosted is irrelevant; the defining idea is warehouse-style tables over open files in a lake.
That two-copy lake-plus-warehouse design is exactly what the lakehouse was invented to replace.

questions.prompt: An upstream team renames a column. What does a data contract give the consuming pipeline?
choices: A way to block the upstream team's deploys until you have signed off
An agreed, versioned schema, so the breaking change is caught before release
Automatic renaming of that column inside every downstream SQL query
A permanent copy of the old column that is kept for compatibility
questions.explain: A contract turns an implicit dependency into an explicit, tested interface: the producer's CI checks its output against the agreed schema, so a rename becomes a visible version change with a migration period rather than a silent break found in tomorrow's nulls. The consumer should still validate on read and fail loudly if the contract is broken.
explain_choice: A contract is an agreement checked in the producer's own pipeline, not a veto over another team's releases.
Contracts detect and negotiate changes; nothing rewrites your queries for you.
Old fields are kept for an agreed deprecation window, then removed; nothing is kept forever.

questions.prompt: What does log-based change data capture (CDC) read to find new, changed and deleted rows?
choices: The source database's transaction log, deletes included
Triggers that email the pipeline whenever a row is changed
An `updated_at` column, which also shows which rows were deleted
A full copy of each table, compared row by row with yesterday's
questions.explain: Every committed change is already written to the database's log (the WAL in Postgres, the binlog in MySQL) in order, so a reader such as Debezium can stream inserts, updates and deletes without querying the tables. Polling an `updated_at` column misses hard deletes and rows changed twice between polls.
explain_choice: Triggers can capture changes, but they add write cost to the source and nothing about CDC involves email.
A deleted row is gone, so no timestamp is left to poll; this is the classic gap in timestamp-based loading.
Full snapshots and diffs work, but they are the costly approach CDC replaces, rereading every row each run.

questions.prompt: Two consumers in the same Kafka consumer group read a topic with four partitions. What happens?
choices: One consumer reads everything while the other waits on hot standby
The partitions are shared out, so each message goes to one
Messages alternate between the two, one at a time
Both consumers receive every message, doubling the work being done
questions.explain: Within a group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, which tracks its progress as a committed offset; that is how a group scales out while keeping per-partition ordering. Separate groups each get every message, and more consumers than partitions leaves the extra ones idle.
explain_choice: With four partitions both consumers get a share; a consumer sits idle only when there are more consumers than partitions.
Assignment is per partition, not per message, which is what preserves ordering within each partition.
That is what happens with two different consumer groups; within one group the work is shared.

questions.prompt: A warehouse bills per byte scanned. Which change cuts a query's cost the most?
choices: Selecting only the columns you need instead of `SELECT *`
Adding `LIMIT 10`, since far fewer rows are sent back to you
Sorting the results so the engine can stop reading early
Running it overnight, when the warehouse's rates are lower
questions.explain: Columnar warehouses read and charge only for the columns a query touches, so dropping unused wide columns shrinks the bill directly. `LIMIT` is applied after the scan and usually saves nothing; partition and cluster pruning are the other big levers.
explain_choice: The engine still scans every referenced column in full before it trims the output, so the bill barely moves.
Sorting adds work after the scan; it does not let the engine skip reading data.
Per-byte pricing does not change with the time of day; scanning less is what lowers the charge.

questions.prompt: What makes a decision a 'one-way door'?
choices: It touches security, so it needs a security review first
Reversing it later would be very costly, or impossible
It must be made quickly, leaving no time for proper review
It needs sign-off from a single named owner before it ships
questions.explain: How much deliberation a decision deserves should scale with the cost of undoing it. Data models, public APIs and vendor lock-in are expensive to reverse, so they earn slow, careful thought; most other choices can be changed cheaply and should be made quickly. Treating every decision as one-way is its own failure: slow teams.
explain_choice: Security matters, but the term is about the cost of reversal, whatever the topic.
Urgency and reversibility are separate; an urgent choice can be easy to undo, and a slow one hard.
Who approves a decision is a process question; the door metaphor is about whether you can walk back through.

questions.prompt: What does 'choose boring technology' actually advise?
choices: Prefer the standard library over any third-party package at all
Never adopt a tool until it has been around for at least ten years
Use the most popular tool in every category, whatever the need
Spend a small novelty budget only where it gives a real advantage
questions.explain: Each unfamiliar component brings failure modes nobody on the team has seen yet, and those surface under pressure, often at 3am. Well-understood tools have known limits and answers already written down, so novelty is kept for the few places where it is the product's edge.
explain_choice: Mature third-party libraries are often the boring choice; the advice is about familiarity, not the stdlib.
The advice is a budget, not a ban; new tools are fine where their benefit outweighs the unknowns they bring.
Popularity is a rough proxy at best; boring means well understood by your team for this job.

questions.prompt: What does a blameless postmortem focus on?
choices: Finding which engineer made the error so they can be retrained
A short timeline of the incident, so the team can quickly move on
The conditions that let the failure happen, and what prevents a repeat
Nothing actionable, since blameless means without consequences
questions.explain: People who fear blame hide mistakes and near misses, and hidden information produces repeat incidents. Treating the human error as a symptom leads to asking why the system allowed it, which yields fixes that last: guard rails, alerts, safer defaults, each with an owner and a deadline.
explain_choice: Singling out a person teaches everyone to hide errors, and leaves the conditions that caused it in place.
A timeline is the raw material, not the output; the value is in the analysis of why it happened.
Blameless does not mean actionless; it produces concrete follow-up fixes, just aimed at systems rather than people.

questions.prompt: What is the expand-migrate-contract pattern for?
choices: Changing a schema with no downtime by serving old and new side by side
Making the whole schema change in one transaction in a maintenance window
Growing a table's capacity before a traffic spike, then shrinking it
Archiving old rows to shrink the database before a risky migration
questions.explain: Old and new versions of the application run at the same time during a deploy, so the schema must suit both. Add the new shape, write to both and backfill, switch reads, and only then drop the old; each step is small, deployable on its own and reversible.
explain_choice: One big change in a window is the downtime the pattern exists to avoid.
The 'expand' is the schema gaining the new shape, not capacity; it has nothing to do with scaling.
The pattern keeps the data; it is about reshaping a schema safely, not reducing its size.

questions.prompt: Why is an SLO useful to a team?
choices: It targets 100% availability, so that every failure is treated as urgent
It replaces alerting, since the team just reviews it once a month
It sets how much unreliability is fine, so trade-offs are explicit
It is a contract with customers, with refunds whenever it is missed
questions.explain: Setting a target below 100% leaves an error budget: the unreliability you can spend on releases and experiments. While budget remains you ship; when it is spent you stabilise. That turns 'ship or fix?' from an argument into arithmetic.
explain_choice: A 100% target leaves no error budget, so every change becomes a threat and delivery stops.
Alerts on budget burn rate are driven by the SLO; it tells monitoring what matters, it does not replace it.
A contract with penalties is an SLA; the SLO is the internal target, usually set stricter than the SLA.

questions.prompt: What is the best evidence of ability beyond senior level?
choices: Breadth: knowing many frameworks well enough to use any of them
Certifications and job titles, which anyone can check independently
Years of experience, which bring good judgement with them over time
Sound judgement on ambiguous problems, in work others rely on
questions.explain: Ambiguous problems arrive without a specification, so the hard part is framing them: which constraint matters, what to leave out, which risk to take first. Other people building on your work is an outside test of those calls holding up in real use, which a count of years, frameworks or certificates cannot show.
explain_choice: Frameworks are interchangeable tools; knowing which problem to solve with them is the scarce part.
Credentials show that material was studied, not that decisions made under uncertainty turned out well.
Years only help if they were spent reflecting on outcomes; ten years can be one year repeated ten times.

questions.prompt: When mentoring someone stuck on a bug, what usually helps them most?
choices: Ask the question that leads them to find the fix themselves
Write the fix for them, so they can see what good looks like
Stay out of it until review, then list everything wrong
Point them to the relevant documentation and step back
questions.explain: Finding the answer themselves builds the method, which transfers to every future bug, and retrieval under a little difficulty is what makes learning stick. A good question narrows the search without removing the struggle, so they keep ownership of the solution.
explain_choice: A worked fix teaches this one answer, and they stay dependent on you for the next bug.
Late, bulk criticism arrives after the learning moment and discourages rather than guides.
Documentation without direction often leaves them searching blind; a question focuses where to look.

questions.prompt: You built something and nobody uses it. What is the right response?
choices: Promote it harder, since people won't use what they haven't seen
Find out why, and be willing to shut it down on the evidence
Add the features users asked for, then relaunch it
Rewrite it on a better stack so it is ready when users arrive
questions.explain: Unused software still costs maintenance, attention and security exposure. Talking to intended users separates a discovery problem from a value problem; if the need is not real, stopping frees the effort for something that matters, and sunk cost is not a reason to continue.
explain_choice: Promotion helps only if the problem is awareness, which you cannot know without asking.
Features requested by people who still do not use it rarely change that; first learn why they do not.
The stack is rarely why nobody uses a product; a rewrite spends more on something unproven.

quizzes.name: Final-boss ladder
quizzes.desc: Building what other software stands on.

questions.prompt: Your HTTP server receives a request with `Content-Length: 12`. How should it find where the body ends?
choices: Keep reading until the client closes the connection
Take one `recv()` call's worth, which returns the whole request
Read exactly 12 bytes after the blank line ending the headers
Read up to the next newline, since each request body is one line
questions.explain: TCP delivers a byte stream with no message boundaries, so HTTP marks them itself: headers end at the first empty line and Content-Length (or chunked encoding) says how many body bytes follow. A server must buffer across as many reads as that takes, and must not wait for a close on a keep-alive connection.
explain_choice: On a keep-alive connection the client stays open for its next request, so waiting for a close hangs both sides.
`recv` returns whatever has arrived so far, which may be part of a request or more than one.
Bodies such as JSON or file uploads can contain any number of newlines; only the declared length is reliable.

questions.prompt: Your mini database adds a B-tree index on `email`. What does that index cost you?
choices: Every insert and update now also has to write to the index
Nothing at all, since an index just makes lookups faster
Lookups by email get slower, since the index is checked first
The table is rewritten, sorted by email, on every new insert
questions.explain: An index is a second, sorted structure that must stay consistent with the table, so each write updates both and takes extra space. It turns a lookup from a full O(n) scan into an O(log n) descent, which is the trade the query planner weighs when choosing whether to use it.
explain_choice: Indexes speed up reads by adding work to writes and using storage; that cost is why you do not index every column.
The index replaces a full scan with a short tree descent, so lookups by email get faster.
Only the index is kept sorted; the table rows stay where they are and the index points at them.

questions.prompt: In your language interpreter, what does the parser turn the token stream into?
choices: Machine code, which the CPU then executes straight away
The source text again, with comments and blanks removed
Tokens: keywords, names and numbers split out of the text
An abstract syntax tree, which the interpreter walks
questions.explain: The lexer groups characters into tokens; the parser applies the grammar to those tokens and builds a tree whose shape encodes precedence and nesting, so `1 + 2 * 3` has the multiplication below the addition. A tree-walking interpreter evaluates that tree node by node.
explain_choice: Generating machine code is a compiler back end's job, several stages after parsing, and many interpreters never do it.
Stripping comments is a lexing detail; the parser's output is structure, not cleaned-up text.
Splitting text into tokens is the lexer's job, which happens before the parser runs.

questions.prompt: Many workers fail against the same service. Why add random jitter to their retry delays?
choices: So the retries look less like an attack to the service's firewall
So workers that failed together don't retry in lockstep
Most message queues reject retries that use a fixed, equal delay
It makes sure each task is attempted exactly once overall
questions.explain: Workers that fail at the same moment and use the same backoff schedule retry in lockstep, hitting a recovering service with synchronised bursts that can knock it over again. Randomising each delay spreads the retries out; idempotent task handlers are what make the retries themselves safe.
explain_choice: The point is load shape, not disguise; synchronised retries harm a recovering service whatever a firewall thinks of them.
Queues accept any retry delay; jitter is a choice made for the downstream service's sake.
Jitter changes when retries happen, not how many; exactly-once effects come from idempotent handling.

questions.prompt: An agent in your AI platform can call a delete-file tool. Where must the permission check live?
choices: In the system prompt, telling the model never to delete files
In the model's reasoning, by asking it to check first
In the tool's own code, which the model can never bypass
In the eval suite, which catches unsafe calls before release
questions.explain: A model's output can be steered by anything in its context, including injected text in retrieved documents, so instructions are advice rather than enforcement.
