Authorisation belongs in deterministic code at the tool boundary, where it applies to every call regardless of what the model was persuaded to request.
explain_choice: A prompt is guidance the model can be talked out of, for example by instructions injected in a retrieved document.
Self-checking is still the model deciding; a manipulated model will happily confirm its own bad call.
Evals measure behaviour offline on sample inputs; they do not stop a live call at run time.

questions.prompt: Faced with an unfamiliar problem, what should you build first?
choices: The complete architecture, so later pieces have a place to fit
Full test coverage for the parts you already understand well
The easiest component, to build momentum before the hard parts
A prototype of the assumption most likely to sink the whole project
questions.explain: Work on the familiar parts cannot tell you whether the project is feasible; the riskiest unknown can. Testing it first, cheaply, either removes the biggest uncertainty or kills the idea before much has been spent, and its result often decides the architecture.
explain_choice: An architecture chosen before the risky unknowns are tested is a guess, and often the wrong one.
Tests for well-understood code reduce little risk; the unknowns are where failure hides.
Momentum on easy parts can end in finding out the hard part is impossible after most of the effort is spent.

questions.prompt: What is a thin vertical slice?
choices: One layer, such as the database, fully built before the rest
One narrow feature working end to end through every layer
An interface mock-up with no working back end behind it
The smallest release that still includes every planned feature
questions.explain: Running one real path through the interface, logic, storage and deployment exposes integration problems in week one rather than month three, and gives you something working to measure and demonstrate. Features are then added as further slices on a skeleton that is already proven.
explain_choice: Building layer by layer defers integration, which is where most surprises live; that is a horizontal slice.
A mock-up tests the look but none of the layers underneath, so it proves nothing about the system.
Including every feature is the opposite of thin; a slice is one feature, deep rather than wide.

questions.prompt: What makes an architecture decision record useful a year later?
choices: It records the context and the options rejected, not only the choice
Every engineer signs it, so the choice can't be reopened afterwards
It is edited in place whenever the decision changes, so it stays current
It describes the final design in enough detail to regenerate the code
questions.explain: The code already shows what was chosen; what gets lost is why, under which constraints, and what was ruled out. With that context a later reader can tell whether the reasons still hold. A changed decision gets a new record that supersedes the old one, so the history of reasoning survives.
explain_choice: Decisions should be reopened when the context changes; the record makes that easier, not impossible.
Records are kept unchanged and superseded by new ones, so the reasoning at each point in time is preserved.
A design specification is a different document; an ADR is short and centres on the reasoning behind one decision.

certs.name: CS50P — Introduction to Programming with Python
certs.what: The best-taught beginner Python course that exists. Nine problem sets and a final project.
certs.worth: High. Real teaching, real problem sets, and the free certificate is genuinely from Harvard.

certs.name: Python Programming MOOC
certs.what: Text-based, brutally exercise-heavy, 5+5 ECTS. Covers OOP, testing, and databases.
certs.worth: High if you learn by doing. The exercise volume is what forces fluency.

certs.name: Scientific Computing with Python
certs.what: Five graded projects: arithmetic formatter, time calculator, budget app, polygon area, probability calculator.
certs.worth: High. The projects are public and verifiable, which is why employers weigh it above badge-farms.

certs.name: Python Essentials 1
certs.what: Syntax through functions, collections, and exceptions. Prepares for the PCEP exam.
certs.worth: Medium. Fast, structured, and the badge is free — good for a résumé line early on.

certs.name: Python Essentials 2
certs.what: Modules, packages, OOP, exceptions, files, and the standard library. Prepares for PCAP.
certs.worth: Medium. Solid intermediate coverage at zero cost.

certs.name: PCEP — Certified Entry-Level Python Programmer
certs.what: Vendor-neutral entry certification. Take it after Python Essentials 1 if you want the credential.
certs.worth: Low-medium. Recognized, but a portfolio beats it. Skip unless an employer names it.

certs.name: PCAP — Certified Associate in Python Programming
certs.what: Modules, OOP, exceptions, file handling, and standard library depth.
certs.worth: Low-medium. Same caveat, higher price. Only worth it if it's a hiring requirement.

certs.name: HackerRank Skills Certification — Python
certs.what: A timed coding assessment. Pass and you get a shareable certificate.
certs.worth: Medium. Cheap signal, and useful as a self-check under time pressure.

certs.name: Kaggle Learn micro-courses
certs.what: Python, pandas, intro ML, intermediate ML, feature engineering, deep learning.
certs.worth: Medium-high for data work. Short, practical, and they stack quickly.

certs.name: Data Analysis with Python
certs.what: NumPy, pandas, and five analysis projects.
certs.worth: Medium-high. Good structure for the data half of the roadmap.

certs.name: Machine Learning with Python
certs.what: TensorFlow-based ML with five graded projects.
certs.worth: Medium. Take Karpathy and fast.ai for depth; take this for the credential.

certs.name: Hugging Face AI Agents Course
certs.what: smolagents, LlamaIndex, and LangGraph side by side, ending in a benchmarked capstone.
certs.worth: High for agent work. The certificate requires shipping running code, not passing a quiz.

certs.name: Hugging Face LLM Course
certs.what: Transformers, fine-tuning, and the Hugging Face stack across 12 chapters.
certs.worth: High if you'll ever touch a model beyond an API call.

certs.name: Hugging Face MCP Course
certs.what: Model Context Protocol — how tools and context get wired into models.
certs.worth: Medium-high and rising. This is where agent tooling is standardizing.

certs.name: Anthropic Academy

certs.worth: High if you're building on Claude specifically.

certs.name: Machine Learning Crash Course

certs.name: MIT 6.S191 — Introduction to Deep Learning
certs.what: University-grade deep learning, refreshed every year, with Colab labs.

certs.name: CS50 AI with Python

certs.name: CS50 Web Programming with Python and JavaScript
certs.what: Django, SQL, JavaScript, front ends, testing, and deployment.
certs.worth: Medium-high if you want the full-stack half.

certs.worth: Medium-high. Strong brand recognition; apply for financial aid rather than paying.
